Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 1–3:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. It is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority of scholars. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: except for three verses of it, which were revealed in Medina, and they are: "And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity" up to His saying: "And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful." Al-Dahhak said: it is Medinan, and among it are Meccan verses, namely His saying: "And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity," and the verses that follow. The purpose of this surah is to mention the greatness of the Qur'an, and to mention the slanders of the disbelievers against prophethood, and to refute their claims, among which is their saying that the Qur'an was fabricated by Muhammad and that it is not from Allah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds. (1) To whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He has not taken a son, and He has no partner in dominion, and He created everything and determined it with precise determination. (2) And they have taken, besides Him, deities that create nothing, while they are themselves created, and they possess not for themselves any harm or benefit, and they possess not death or life or resurrection. (3)﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion﴾. "Tabaraka" (blessed, exalted) — its meaning has been disputed. Al-Farra' said: in the Arabic language it is equivalent to "taqaddasa" (sanctified), and both denote greatness. Al-Zajjaj said: "tabaraka" is of the form "tafa"ala" from "al-barakah" (blessing). He said: the meaning of blessing is abundance from every possessor of good. It was said: "tabaraka" means "ta'ala" (exalted). It was said: His bounty is exalted, i.e., increased and multiplied. It was said: the meaning is that His favour endures and is established. Al-Nahhas said: this is the most appropriate of these in linguistics and derivation, from "baraka al-shay'" when it became firm, and from it comes "baraka al-jamal wa al-tair 'ala al-ma'" (the camel and the bird settled upon the water), i.e., it remained and was firm. As for the first view, it is confused, because sanctification is only from purity, and it has nothing to do with this. Al-Tha'labi said: it is said "Tabaraka Allah," and it is not said "mutabarak" or "mubarak," because one stops in His names and attributes at the point where revelation has come (tawqif). Al-Tirimmah said:

Blessed are You; none gives what You have withheld,
and none withholds what You have given, O Lord.

Another said:

Blessed are You; whatever You decree comes to pass, and to You belongs thanks.

I say: some scholars have mentioned among His Most Beautiful Names "al-Mubarak" (the Blessed), and we have also mentioned it in our book. If there is agreement that it is not said, then it is accepted by consensus. If there is disagreement about it, then many of the names have been disputed regarding their enumeration, such as "al-Dahr" (time) and others. We have drawn attention to this there, and praise be to Allah. "Al-Furqan" is the Qur'an. It was said: it is a name for every revealed scripture, as He said: ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion﴾ [see vol. 11, p. 295]. Regarding its being named "Furqan," there are two views: first, because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and between the believer and the disbeliever. Second, because in it is the explanation of what was legislated of lawful and unlawful; this is related from al-Naqqash.

(upon His servant) meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

(that he may be a warner to the worlds) The subject of "yakun" (may be) is a pronoun referring to "'abdihi" (His servant), and this is preferable because it is closer to it. It is also permissible that it refers to "al-Furqan." 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr read "'ala 'ibadihi" (upon His servants). It is said: "andhara" means "kharrafa" (to warn, to frighten), and it has been discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 184, second or third edition]. "Al-Nadhir" is one who warns against destruction. Al-Jawhari said: "al-Nadhir" is the one who warns, and "al-Nadhir" is the warning. The intended meaning of "al-'Alamin" here is humankind and jinn, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was a messenger to both of them and a warner to both of them, and he is the Seal of the Prophets. No one other than him had a universal message except Nuh, for he extended his message to all of humankind after the Flood, since creation began with him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: He exalted Himself.

(He has not taken a son) He, glorified and exalted, declared Himself free of what the polytheists said, that the angels are the children of Allah, meaning the daughters of Allah, glorified and exalted is He. And of what the Jews said: 'Uzayr is the son of Allah, exalted is Allah. And of what the Christians said: the Messiah is the son of Allah, Allah is exalted above that.

(and He has no partner in the dominion) as the idolaters said.

(and He created everything) not as the Magians and the Dualists said, that Satan or darkness creates some things. Nor as one who says: the created being has the power of origination. So the verse is a refutation of these.

(and determined it with precise determination) meaning He determined everything He created by His wisdom according to what He willed, not out of forgetfulness or heedlessness; rather, the decrees proceed according to what Allah created until the Day of Resurrection, and after the Resurrection. So He is the Creator, the Determiner (in one copy: "al-Muqtadir," the Powerful), so worship Him alone.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they have taken, besides Him, deities﴾: He mentioned what the polytheists did, in a manner of wonder, in their taking of deities, despite the evidence He has manifested of His oneness and power.

(that create nothing) meaning the deities.

(while they are themselves created) Since the polytheists believed of them that they harm and benefit, He described them as one describes those who have intellect.

(and they possess not for themselves any harm or benefit) that is, they possess neither the repelling of harm nor the bringing of benefit; so the object has been omitted. It was said: they are not able to harm themselves or benefit them with anything, nor those who worship them, because they are inanimate.

(and they possess not death or life or resurrection) that is, they cause no one to die and do not give life to anyone. "Al-Nushur" is the revival after death; Allah "anshara" the dead and they were "nushirū" (raised). This has been discussed earlier [see vol. 7, p. 229, first or second edition]. Al-A'sha said:

Until people say, at what they have seen:
"How strange, the dead one raised up!"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 4–6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾, meaning the polytheists of Quraysh. Ibn Abbas said: the one who said this among them was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and likewise everything in the Quran that mentions al-asatir (myths). Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: he used to harm the Prophet ﷺ.

(﴿This is not but a falsehood﴾) meaning the Quran.

(﴿A falsehood he has invented﴾) i.e., a lie he has fabricated.

(﴿And other people helped him with it﴾) meaning the Jews, as related by Mujahid. Ibn Abbas said: by His saying "other people" is meant Abu Fukayha, a freedman of the Banu al-Hadrami, and Addas and Jabr, and these three were from the People of the Book. Their mention has already passed in Surat al-Nahl [[See vol. 10, p. 177 ff. of this edition, first or second printing.]].

(﴿Then they have produced an injustice﴾) i.e., with injustice. It was also said: the meaning is "then they have come with injustice."

(﴿And falsehood. And they say: "Tales of the former peoples"﴾) Al-Zajjaj said: the singular of al-asatir is ustura, like uhdutha and ahadith. Others said: asatir is the plural of Asthar, like aqwal and aqawil.

(﴿He has had them written down﴾) meaning Muhammad.

(﴿So they are dictated to him morning and evening﴾) i.e., they are recited and read to him, until they are memorized.

The word tumla (تُمْلى) originally was tumlal, and the final lam was changed to a ya' because of the doubling (idgham), as in their saying taqadda al-bazi and similar.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "He has sent it down who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth"﴾, i.e., say, O Muhammad: He who knows the secret has sent down this Quran, so He is the knower of the unseen, and therefore He has no need of a teacher. The mention of "the secret" rather than "the open" is because whoever knows the secret knows the open even better. And if the Quran had been taken from the People of the Book and others, it would not have gone beyond them, but it came with arts that lie outside them, so it was not taken from them. Also, if it had been taken from these people, the polytheists would have been able to obtain it just as Muhammad ﷺ did, so why did they not produce a counterpart? Thus their objection is refuted in every respect.

(﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾) meaning: Forgiving to His allies and Merciful to them.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 25, verses 7–8:**

﴿And they say, "What is this messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ There are two issues (masa'il) here.

The first issue concerns God's words, ﴿And they said﴾. He mentions another of their slanders. The pronoun in "qalu" (they said) refers to the Quraysh. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 9–10:

Allah's saying: ﴿Look how they coined for you the parables﴾, meaning: they coined these parables for you in order to reach your denial.

(So they went astray) from the path of truth and from attaining what they intended.

(So they cannot find a way) to correct what they said about you.

Allah's saying: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. This is a conditional sentence with its response. "Ja'ala lak" was not assimilated (idghам) because the two words are separate; assimilation is permissible because the two identical letters meet.

(Wa yaj'al lak) is in a jussive position (mawdi' jazm), conjoined by coordination (ʿatf) to the position of "ja'ala". It may also be in a nominative position (mawdi' raf'), detached from the first clause, and the people of Syria (Ahl al-Sham) recited it this way. It is also transmitted from ʿAsim: "wa yaj'alu lak" with a nominative vowel, meaning: "and He will give you palaces in the Hereafter." Mujahid said: Quraysh used to regard a house built of stone as a palace (qasr), whatever it was. The word "qasr" in the language means confinement, and a palace is called qasr because whoever is in it is kept (maqsur) from being reached. It was also said: the Arabs call houses of clay "qasr," and what is made of wool and hair is called "bayt" (house). This was related by al-Qushayri. Sufyan narrated from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Khaythama, who said: It was said to the Prophet ﷺ: "If you wish, We will give you the treasures of this world and its keys, which were not given to anyone before you and will not be given to anyone after you, and that will not diminish anything of your reward in the Hereafter; or if you wish, We will gather all that for you in the Hereafter." He said: "Let it be gathered for me in the Hereafter." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He will give you palaces﴾.

It is also reported that this verse was brought down by Ridwan, the keeper of the Gardens, to the Prophet ﷺ. In the report: When Ridwan descended, he greeted the Prophet ﷺ and then said: "O Muhammad! The Lord of Might sends you His greetings, and this is a casket [al-safat: a container in which perfume and similar women's articles are kept. It was also said: like a sack. In one manuscript: "sawt" (whip), which is a distortion] — and behold, a casket of light, shining — your Lord says to you: these are the keys to the treasures of the world, though this will not reduce your possessions in the Hereafter by the weight of a gnat's wing." The Prophet ﷺ looked at Jibril as one seeking his counsel, and Jibril struck the earth with his hand, indicating: be humble. So he said: "O Ridwan, I have no need for it. Poverty is dearer to me, and that I be a patient, grateful servant." Ridwan said: "You have done well! May Allah grant it to you." And he mentioned the hadith.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 11–14:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, but they denied the Hour﴾ — He means the Day of Resurrection.

(And We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blazing Fire) — He means Jahannam (Hell), blazing against them.

(When it sees them from a distant place) — i.e., from a distance of five hundred years.

(They will hear its raging and its roaring) — It has been said: the meaning is that when Jahannam sees them, they hear the sound of its rage against them. It has also been said: the meaning is that when its keepers see them, they hear from them raging and roaring, out of eagerness for their punishment. The first view is more sound, because of what has been related with a raised (marfu') chain that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat between the two eyes of Jahannam." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah! Does it have two eyes?" He said: "Have you not heard Allah, Mighty and Majestic, say: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and its roaring﴾? A neck will come out of the Fire, having two eyes that see and a tongue that speaks, and it will say: 'I have been charged with everyone who set up another god with Allah.' It is keener to see them than a bird is to see sesame seeds, and it will pick them up." In another narration: "A neck will come out of the Fire and snatch up the disbelievers as a bird snatches up sesame seeds." Razin mentioned it in his book, and Ibn al-'Arabi affirmed its soundness in his Qabas, and said: that is, it separates them from the creation in recognition, as a bird separates sesame seeds from the dust. al-Tirmidhi also transmitted it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A neck will come out of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, having two eyes that see, two ears that hear, and a tongue that speaks, saying: 'I have been charged with three: every tyrannical obstinate one, everyone who called upon another god besides Allah, and the image-makers.'" And on this subject there is a report from Abu Sa'id. Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: this is a hasan, gharib, sahih hadith. Al-Kalbi said: they hear from it raging like the raging of the children of Adam and a sound like the braying of a donkey. It has also been said: there is inversion in the verse; the meaning is: they hear from it roaring and know its raging. Qutrub said: raging is not heard, but seen; the meaning is: they see from it raging and hear from it roaring, like the saying of the poet:

"And I saw your husband among the people [[So the originals have it, and it is correct. In the printed edition: al-Wara]] ... girded with a sword and a spear"

That is, carrying a spear. It has also been said: "they heard for it" means "in it," i.e., they heard in it raging and roaring against the tormented. As Allah the Exalted said: ﴿For them therein is groaning and wailing﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 90, first or second edition.]]. The letters "fi" (in) and "li" (for) are close in meaning: you say, "I do this in Allah" and "for Allah."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when they are cast into a narrow place therein, bound together﴾ — Qatadah said: It was mentioned to us that 'Abd Allah used to say: Indeed Jahannam is narrowed upon the disbeliever like the narrowing of the zajj (the iron point at the lower end of a spear) upon the spear. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned it in his Raqa'iq. Likewise Ibn 'Abbas said, which al-Tha'labi and al-Qushayri related from him, and al-Mawardi related it from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr. The meaning of "muqarranin" (bound together) is "shackled," as said by Abu Salih. It has also been said: fettered, their hands tied to their necks in chains. It has also been said: they are bound together with the devils, i.e., each one of them is bound to his devil, as said by Yahya ibn Salam. This has already passed in (the commentary on) "Ibrahim" [[See vol. 9, p. 384, first or second edition.]]. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"They returned with plunder and captives... and we returned with kings bound together [[The narration in the verse is: "musaffidina" (fettered).]]"

(There they cry out for destruction) — i.e., ruin, said by al-Dahhak. Ibn 'Abbas: "Woe." And it is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The first to say it is Iblis, because he is the first who will be clothed in a garment of Fire, placed upon his brows, and he will drag it behind him, and his offspring behind him, and he will be saying: 'Woe to me!'" It is in the accusative as a verbal noun, i.e., "we perished a perishing," said by al-Zajjaj. Others said: it is an object.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction, but call out for many destructions﴾ — for your ruin is greater than that you should call out only once. He said: "thubur" is a verbal noun which applies to few and many, therefore it is not pluralized, and it is like your saying: "I struck him a great striking," and "he sat a long sitting." The verses were revealed concerning Ibn Khatal and his companions.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, but they denied the Hour﴾ — He means the Day of Resurrection.

(And We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blazing Fire) — He means Jahannam (Hell), blazing against them.

(When it sees them from a distant place) — i.e., from a distance of five hundred years.

(They will hear its raging and its roaring) — It has been said: the meaning is that when Jahannam sees them, they hear the sound of its rage against them. It has also been said: the meaning is that when its keepers see them, they hear from them raging and roaring, out of eagerness for their punishment. The first view is more sound, because of what has been related with a raised (marfu') chain that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat between the two eyes of Jahannam." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah! Does it have two eyes?" He said: "Have you not heard Allah, Mighty and Majestic, say: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and its roaring﴾? A neck will come out of the Fire, having two eyes that see and a tongue that speaks, and it will say: 'I have been charged with everyone who set up another god with Allah.' It is keener to see them than a bird is to see sesame seeds, and it will pick them up." In another narration: "A neck will come out of the Fire and snatch up the disbelievers as a bird snatches up sesame seeds." Razin mentioned it in his book, and Ibn al-'Arabi affirmed its soundness in his Qabas, and said: that is, it separates them from the creation in recognition, as a bird separates sesame seeds from the dust. al-Tirmidhi also transmitted it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A neck will come out of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, having two eyes that see, two ears that hear, and a tongue that speaks, saying: 'I have been charged with three: every tyrannical obstinate one, everyone who called upon another god besides Allah, and the image-makers.'" And on this subject there is a report from Abu Sa'id. Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: this is a hasan, gharib, sahih hadith. Al-Kalbi said: they hear from it raging like the raging of the children of Adam and a sound like the braying of a donkey. It has also been said: there is inversion in the verse; the meaning is: they hear from it roaring and know its raging. Qutrub said: raging is not heard, but seen; the meaning is: they see from it raging and hear from it roaring, like the saying of the poet:

"And I saw your husband among the people [[So the originals have it, and it is correct. In the printed edition: al-Wara]] ... girded with a sword and a spear"

That is, carrying a spear. It has also been said: "they heard for it" means "in it," i.e., they heard in it raging and roaring against the tormented. As Allah the Exalted said: ﴿For them therein is groaning and wailing﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 90, first or second edition.]]. The letters "fi" (in) and "li" (for) are close in meaning: you say, "I do this in Allah" and "for Allah."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when they are cast into a narrow place therein, bound together﴾ — Qatadah said: It was mentioned to us that 'Abd Allah used to say: Indeed Jahannam is narrowed upon the disbeliever like the narrowing of the zajj (the iron point at the lower end of a spear) upon the spear. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned it in his Raqa'iq. Likewise Ibn 'Abbas said, which al-Tha'labi and al-Qushayri related from him, and al-Mawardi related it from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr. The meaning of "muqarranin" (bound together) is "shackled," as said by Abu Salih. It has also been said: fettered, their hands tied to their necks in chains. It has also been said: they are bound together with the devils, i.e., each one of them is bound to his devil, as said by Yahya ibn Salam. This has already passed in (the commentary on) "Ibrahim" [[See vol. 9, p. 384, first or second edition.]]. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"They returned with plunder and captives... and we returned with kings bound together [[The narration in the verse is: "musaffidina" (fettered).]]"

(There they cry out for destruction) — i.e., ruin, said by al-Dahhak. Ibn 'Abbas: "Woe." And it is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The first to say it is Iblis, because he is the first who will be clothed in a garment of Fire, placed upon his brows, and he will drag it behind him, and his offspring behind him, and he will be saying: 'Woe to me!'" It is in the accusative as a verbal noun, i.e., "we perished a perishing," said by al-Zajjaj. Others said: it is an object.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction, but call out for many destructions﴾ — for your ruin is greater than that you should call out only once. He said: "thubur" is a verbal noun which applies to few and many, therefore it is not pluralized, and it is like your saying: "I struck him a great striking," and "he sat a long sitting." The verses were revealed concerning Ibn Khatal and his companions.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 15–16:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of eternity which the God-fearing have been promised?"﴾ If it is said: how can He say "Is that better" when there is no good at all in the Fire? The answer is that Sibawayh related from the Arabs: "Is misery more beloved to you, or happiness?" – though it is known that happiness is more beloved to him. It has also been said: this is not of the type of "afal" (the comparative form) "than you," but rather like your saying: "He has good (khayr) with him." Al-Nahhas said: this is a good opinion, just as [[It is Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him, praising the Prophet ﷺ and satirizing Abu Sufyan; the first half of the verse is: "Do you satirize, while you are no match for him?"]] said:

"So which of you two is better as a ransom (fida')?"

It was said: He only said that because Paradise and Hell have both entered the category of abodes, so He spoke this way to indicate the difference between the two abodes. It has also been said: this is a response to His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that﴾, to the end of the verse. It has also been said: it is a response to His saying: ﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him, or he have a garden from which he eats﴾. It has also been said: He only said that in the sense of your knowledge and belief, O disbelievers, for when they were doing the deeds of the people of the Fire, they became as though they were saying that there is good in the Fire.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾, that is, of bliss.

(﴿They will abide eternally. It is ever for your Lord a promise that is asked for.﴾) Al-Kalbi said: Allah promised the believers Paradise as a reward for their deeds, so they asked Him for that promise, saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Abbas. It has also been said: the angels ask Paradise for them, its evidence being His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eternity which You have promised them﴾, to the end of the verse. This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. It has also been said: the meaning of "a promise that is asked for" is that it is binding, even though it is not actually requested, like a debt; it is related from the Arabs: "I will certainly give you a thousand." It has also been said: "a promise that is asked for" means that it is owed to you, so you ask for it. Zayd ibn Aslam said: they asked Allah for Paradise in this world and turned to Him in supplication, so He answered them in the Hereafter with what they had asked for and gave them what they sought. This returns to the first view.

**Verse 17:** ﴿And on the Day He gathers them﴾. Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Ibn Kathir, Hafs, Ya'qub, and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Duri read "يَحْشُرُهُمْ" with a *yāʾ* (the verb in the third person). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, because of His saying at the beginning of the passage, ﴿was upon your Lord﴾, and at its end, ﴿Did you lead these, My servants, astray, or did they stray from the way themselves?﴾. The rest read it with a *nūn* (the first person plural), as an expression of exaltedness (*taʿẓīm*).

﴿And those they worshipped besides Allah﴾: from among the angels, humans, jinn, the Messiah, and ʿUzayr. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj. Al-Dahhak and Ikrimah said it refers to the idols.

﴿Then He will say﴾: the common reading is with a *yāʾ*, and this is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Haywah read it with a *nūn*, as an expression of exaltedness.

﴿Did you lead these, My servants, astray, or did they stray from the way themselves?﴾ This is a rhetorical question of rebuke to the disbelievers.

﴿They will say: Glory be to You﴾, that is, the objects of worship besides Allah will say, "Glory be to You," meaning, exalting You above any partner, ﴿it was not for us to take any protectors besides You﴾. If it is asked: if the idols that were worshipped are gathered, how can they speak while they are inanimate? It is answered: Allah will make them speak on the Day of Resurrection, just as He makes the hands and feet speak.

Al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far read "أَنْ نُتَّخَذَ" (*an nuttakhaḏa*) with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* and a *fatḥa* on the *khāʾ*, as a passive verb. The grammarians have discussed this reading. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar said: "nuttakhaḏu" is not permissible. Abu ʿAmr said: if it were "nuttakhaḏa," the second "min" would be deleted, and you would say, "an nuttakhaḏa min dūnika awliyāʾa." Likewise Abu ʿUbayda said: "nuttakhaḏa" is not permissible, because Allah mentioned "min" twice, and if it were as he recited, He would have said, "an nuttakhaḏa min dūnika awliyāʾa." It has also been said that the second "min" is superfluous (*ṣila*). Al-Nahhas said: someone like Abu ʿAmr, despite his eminence and standing, deserves to have what he said approved, because he came with clear evidence. The explanation of what he said is that one may say: "mā ittakhaḏtu rajulan waliyyan" (I did not take a man as a close friend), and this may apply to one specific individual. Then one may say: "mā ittakhaḏtu min rajulin waliyyan," which becomes a general negation. Your saying "waliyyan" follows what precedes it, so "min" cannot enter it, because there is no benefit in that.

﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment﴾, that is, in this world, with health, wealth, and long life, after the death of the messengers, peace be upon them.

﴿Until they forgot the Remembrance﴾, that is, they abandoned Your remembrance and associated others with You out of arrogance and ignorance, so they worshipped us without our having commanded them to do so. Regarding "the Remembrance" there are two views. The first: it is the Qur'an sent down to the messengers; they abandoned acting upon it, as said by Ibn Zayd. The second: it is gratitude for the kindness and favours He bestowed upon them. ﴿They were a people ruined﴾, that is, lost, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas. It derives from *al-bawār*, which is destruction.

Abu al-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him), when he was overlooking the people of Homs, said: "O people of Homs! Come to a brother of yours who gives sincere advice." When they gathered around him, he said: "What is wrong with you that you are not ashamed? You build what you will not dwell in, you gather what you will not eat, and you hope for what you will not attain. Those before you built strong buildings, gathered slaves, and cherished far-off hopes; so their gathering became ruin, their hopes became delusion, and their dwellings became graves." So his saying "būran" means lost. In another report: "their dwellings became *būran*," meaning empty, with nothing in them. Al-Hasan said: "būran" means there is no good in them, derived from the ruin of the land, which is leaving it without crops so that nothing good is in it. Shahr ibn Hawshab said: *al-bawār* means corruption and stagnation, derived from the saying, "bārat al-silʿa" when the commodity became unsaleable, like something spoiled. From this is the hadith: "We seek refuge in Allah from the *bawār* of the unmarried woman" (*al-ayyim*). It is an infinitive of the noun type (*ism maṣdar*), like *zūr*, in which the singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine are alike. Ibn al-Zibaʿrā said:

*O Messenger of the King, indeed my tongue*
*mends what I have torn, since I am *būr*.*
*When I contend with the devil in the ways of error,*
*and whoever inclines to his inclination is one destroyed.*

Some said: the singular is *bāʾir*, and the plural is *būr*, as one says "ʿāʾidh" and "ʿawdh," and "hāʾid" and "hūd." It has also been said: "būran" means blind to the truth.

**Verse 19:** ﴿So they have denied you in what you say﴾. That is, Allah says, when the objects of worship disown their worshippers: ﴿So they have denied you in what you say﴾, that is, in your claim that they are gods.

﴿Nor can they avert [punishment]﴾, meaning the gods cannot turn the punishment away from you, nor help you. It has also been said: the disbelievers, when the objects of worship deny them, cannot avert punishment ("ṣarfan") nor obtain help ("naṣran") from Allah. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that these disbelievers, O believers, have denied you by what Muhammad brought; and on this view, "bimā taqūlūn" means "by what you say of the truth." Abu ʿUbayd said: the meaning is "fīmā taqūlūn" (in what you say), so they cannot turn you away from the truth to which Allah has guided you, nor can they help themselves against the punishment that descends upon them for denying you.

The common reading is "bimā taqūlūn" with a *tāʾ*, in address. We have already explained its meaning. Al-Farra' reported that he read "faqad kadhdhabūkum" lightly (*mukhaffafan*), "bimā yaqūlūn" (with a *yāʾ*). Likewise Mujahid and al-Bazzi read with a *yāʾ*, and the meaning of "yaqūlūn" is "by their saying." Abu Haywah read "bimā yaqūlūn" with a *yāʾ*, and "famā tastaṭīʿūn" with a *tāʾ*, in address to those who took partners. Whoever reads with a *yāʾ* means: "famā yastaṭīʿu al-shurakāʾ" (the partners cannot).

﴿And whoever among you does wrong﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: whoever among you associates others with Allah and dies in that state.

﴿We will make him taste﴾, that is, in the Hereafter.

﴿a great punishment﴾, that is, a severe one, like His saying, ﴿and you will surely rise to a great exaltation﴾, meaning severe.

Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar said: "nuttakhaḏu" is not permissible. Abu ʿAmr said: if it were "nuttakhaḏa," the second "min" would be deleted, and you would say, "an nuttakhaḏa min dūnika awliyāʾa." Likewise Abu ʿUbayda said: "nuttakhaḏa" is not permissible, because Allah mentioned "min" twice, and if it were as he recited, He would have said, "an nuttakhaḏa min dūnika awliyāʾa." It has also been said that the second "min" is superfluous (*ṣila*). Al-Nahhas said: someone like Abu ʿAmr, despite his eminence and standing, deserves to have what he said approved, because he came with clear evidence. The explanation of what he said is that one may say: "mā ittakhaḏtu rajulan waliyyan" (I did not take a man as a close friend), and this may apply to one specific individual. Then one may say: "mā ittakhaḏtu min rajulin waliyyan," which becomes a general negation. Your saying "waliyyan" follows what precedes it, so "min" cannot enter it, because there is no benefit in that.

﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment﴾, that is, in this world, with health, wealth, and long life, after the death of the messengers, peace be upon them.

﴿Until they forgot the Remembrance﴾, that is, they abandoned Your remembrance and associated others with You out of arrogance and ignorance, so they worshipped us without our having commanded them to do so. Regarding "the Remembrance" there are two views. The first: it is the Qur'an sent down to the messengers; they abandoned acting upon it, as said by Ibn Zayd. The second: it is gratitude for the kindness and favours He bestowed upon them. ﴿They were a people ruined﴾, that is, lost, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas. It derives from *al-bawār*, which is destruction.

Abu al-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him), when he was overlooking the people of Homs, said: "O people of Homs! Come to a brother of yours who gives sincere advice." When they gathered around him, he said: "What is wrong with you that you are not ashamed? You build what you will not dwell in, you gather what you will not eat, and you hope for what you will not attain. Those before you built strong buildings, gathered slaves, and cherished far-off hopes; so their gathering became ruin, their hopes became delusion, and their dwellings became graves." So his saying "būran" means lost. In another report: "their dwellings became *būran*," meaning empty, with nothing in them. Al-Hasan said: "būran" means there is no good in them, derived from the ruin of the land, which is leaving it without crops so that nothing good is in it. Shahr ibn Hawshab said: *al-bawār* means corruption and stagnation, derived from the saying, "bārat al-silʿa" when the commodity became unsaleable, like something spoiled. From this is the hadith: "We seek refuge in Allah from the *bawār* of the unmarried woman" (*al-ayyim*). It is an infinitive of the noun type (*ism maṣdar*), like *zūr*, in which the singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine are alike. Ibn al-Zibaʿrā said:

*O Messenger of the King, indeed my tongue*
*mends what I have torn, since I am *būr*.*
*When I contend with the devil in the ways of error,*
*and whoever inclines to his inclination is one destroyed.*

Some said: the singular is *bāʾir*, and the plural is *būr*, as one says "ʿāʾidh" and "ʿawdh," and "hāʾid" and "hūd." It has also been said: "būran" means blind to the truth.

**Verse 19:** ﴿So they have denied you in what you say﴾. That is, Allah says, when the objects of worship disown their worshippers: ﴿So they have denied you in what you say﴾, that is, in your claim that they are gods.

﴿Nor can they avert [punishment]﴾, meaning the gods cannot turn the punishment away from you, nor help you. It has also been said: the disbelievers, when the objects of worship deny them, cannot avert punishment ("ṣarfan") nor obtain help ("naṣran") from Allah. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that these disbelievers, O believers, have denied you by what Muhammad brought; and on this view, "bimā taqūlūn" means "by what you say of the truth." Abu ʿUbayd said: the meaning is "fīmā taqūlūn" (in what you say), so they cannot turn you away from the truth to which Allah has guided you, nor can they help themselves against the punishment that descends upon them for denying you.

The common reading is "bimā taqūlūn" with a *tāʾ*, in address. We have already explained its meaning. Al-Farra' reported that he read "faqad kadhdhabūkum" lightly (*mukhaffafan*), "bimā yaqūlūn" (with a *yāʾ*). Likewise Mujahid and al-Bazzi read with a *yāʾ*, and the meaning of "yaqūlūn" is "by their saying." Abu Haywah read "bimā yaqūlūn" with a *yāʾ*, and "famā tastaṭīʿūn" with a *tāʾ*, in address to those who took partners. Whoever reads with a *yāʾ* means: "famā yastaṭīʿu al-shurakāʾ" (the partners cannot).

﴿And whoever among you does wrong﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: whoever among you associates others with Allah and dies in that state.

﴿We will make him taste﴾, that is, in the Hereafter.

﴿a great punishment﴾, that is, a severe one, like His saying, ﴿and you will surely rise to a great exaltation﴾, meaning severe.

**Question 1:** Allah's words, ﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾, were revealed in answer to the polytheists when they said, "What is wrong with this messenger, that he eats food and walks in the markets?" Ibn 'Abbas said: When the polytheists reproached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with poverty and said, "What is wrong with this messenger, that he eats food," up to the end of the verse, the Prophet (ﷺ) grieved over that, so this was revealed to console him. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) said: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah! Allah, your Lord, sends you His greetings and says to you: ﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾," meaning, they sought livelihood in this world.

**Question 2:** Allah's words, ﴿Except that they ate food﴾ (إِلَّا إِنَّهُمْ لَيَأْكُلُونَ الطَّعامَ). When the lam (اللَّامُ, the emphatic particle) enters, the إِنَّ (inna) after إِلَّا must be pronounced with a kasra (the vowel i). Even if the lam were not there, only the kasra would be permitted, because the clause is resumptive (مُسْتَأْنَفَةٌ, starting a new sentence). This is the view of all the grammarians. Al-Nahhas said: 'Ali ibn Sulayman related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid, who said: "In this إِنَّ, a fatha is permitted if the lam follows it." I think this was a mistake on his part. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: There is an ellipsis in the sentence, and the meaning is: "And We did not send before you messengers except that they ate food." Then "messengers" (رُسُلًا) was elided, because the phrase "from among the messengers" (مِنَ الْمُرْسَلِينَ) indicates it. So, according to al-Zajjaj, the antecedent noun is elided. He does not permit eliding the relative pronoun and leaving its clause, as al-Farra' said. Al-Farra' said: The elided word is "man" (مَنْ, "whoever"), and the meaning is: "except whoever, indeed they eat food." He compared this to Allah's words, ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾, and His words, ﴿And there is none of you but will pass through it﴾, meaning: there is none of you except whoever will pass through it. This is also the view of al-Kisa'i. The Arabs say: "I have not sent to you any of the people except whoever, indeed he obeys you" (إِنَّهُ لَيُطِيعُكَ). So your saying "indeed he obeys you" is the clause (صِلَةُ) of "man." Al-Zajjaj said: This is an error, because "man" is a relative pronoun, and it is not permissible to elide it. The scholars of meanings (أَهْلُ الْمَعَانِي) said: The meaning is: "And We did not send before you any messengers except that it is said, 'Indeed they eat.'" Its evidence is Allah's words, ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: The إِنَّهُمْ after إِلَّا is pronounced with a kasra for resumption, with an implied waw, meaning: "except, and indeed they..." A group held that His words, "they eat food," are a metonymy for the human need (حَدَث, bodily need). I say: This is eloquent in its meaning. Similar to it is Allah's words, ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was only a messenger; messengers had passed before him; and his mother was a truthful woman. They both used to eat food﴾.

(And they walk in the markets) Al-Jumhur read "yamshuna" (يَمْشُونَ) with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the mim, and a light shin. 'Ali, Ibn 'Awf and Ibn Mas'ud read it with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the mim, and a doubled shin with a fatha, meaning: "they are called to walk and are made to walk." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read it with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the mim, and a damma on the doubled shin, and this has the meaning of "they walk." The poet said:

*"He walked among the camel pens of the watering place and sought*
*from them young she-camels, some difficult and some docile for riding."*

(In the Ruh al-Ma'ani, "docile" [dhalul] is given instead of "for riding" [rakub].)

Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

*"From him the beasts of prey in the open wilderness remain silent,*
*and the men do not walk in his valley."*

(Al-Jaww: the wide open land. Dāmizah: still, silent; every silent one is damiz. Al-Arajil: the plural of arjal, as an'am is the plural of na'am, and arjal is the plural of rajul. The poet describes a lion, saying that the lions and men fear him: the lions are still out of his awe, and the men refrain from walking in his valley.) This has the meaning of "tamashsha" (walks).

**Question 3:** This verse is a foundation for pursuing causes (الْأَسْبَابِ) and seeking livelihood through trade, craft and other means. This meaning has been discussed in more than one place before, but here we will mention enough of it. Some scholars of this time said to me in the course of a conversation: "The prophets (peace be upon them) were sent only to establish causes for the weak." I replied to him: "This is a statement that comes only from the ignorant, the stupid, the vulgar fools, or from someone who slanders the Book and the lofty Sunnah. Allah the Exalted has informed in His Book about His chosen ones, His messengers and prophets, regarding causes and crafts. He, whose word is true, said: ﴿And We taught him the making of armor for you﴾. And He said: ﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets.﴾" The scholars said: That is, they engaged in trade and crafts. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "My provision has been placed under the shade of my spear." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So eat of what you have taken as lawful and good﴾. The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) engaged in trade and crafts, and worked on their properties, and fought those disbelievers who opposed them. Do you think they were weak? Rather, by Allah, they were the strong, and the righteous successors followed them, and their path in this is guidance and right direction. He said: "They only took these up because they were leaders to be followed, so they took them up directly for the sake of the weak, but not for their own sake. The evidence for this is the People of the Suffah (Ashab al-Suffa)." I say: If that were the case, it would have been obligatory for them and for the Messenger with them to explain it, as is established in the Qur'an: ﴿And We revealed to you the Reminder, so that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them﴾. And He said: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance﴾ up to the end of the verse. And this is among the clear proofs and guidance. As for the People of the Suffah, they were guests of Islam in a time of hardship. When sadaqah (charity) came to him (peace be upon him), he would give it specifically to them, and when a gift came to him, he would eat it with them. Yet they used to gather firewood and carry water to the dwellings of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is how al-Bukhari and others described them. Then, when Allah opened the lands to them and made their resting places comfortable, they were given command, and they were ordered to take up causes. Furthermore, this statement indicates the weakness of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, because they were supported by the angels and strengthened by them. If they had been strong, they would not have needed the support of the angels, and that support is itself one of the causes of victory. We seek refuge with Allah from a statement or generalization that leads to this. Rather, the position that causes and means are the Sunnah of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, and it is the clear truth and the straight path on which the consensus (ijma', the scholarly agreement) of the Muslims has been reached. Otherwise, Allah's words, ﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of force and of steeds of war﴾ up to the end of the verse, would have been restricted to the weak, and all such addresses would be the same. In the revelation, when Allah addressed Musa the Interlocutor (al-Kalim): ﴿Strike the sea with your staff﴾, though He was able to split the sea without striking with a staff. Likewise Maryam (peace be upon her): ﴿And shake toward yourself the trunk of the date palm﴾, though He was able to make the ripe dates fall without shaking or effort. Yet with all this, we do not deny that a man may be shown kindness and helped, or his supplication may be answered, or he may be honored with a miracle in his own person or for the sake of others, and the universal principles and beautiful matters are not thereby demolished. Far, far be it! It may not be said: "Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision and what you are promised﴾." We say: "Allah the Mighty has spoken truly, and His noble Messenger has spoken truly. The provision here is the rain, by the consensus of the interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil), based on His words: ﴿And He sends down to you provision from the sky﴾, and He said: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and with it We grew gardens and grain for harvest﴾." No one has witnessed loaves of bread or dishes of meat descending from the sky upon creation. Rather, causes are fundamental to the existence of all this, and this is the meaning of his (peace be upon him) words: "Seek provision in the hidden places of the earth," meaning, through plowing, digging and planting. Something may be named after what it leads to, and rain was called "provision" because provision comes from it, and this is well known in the speech of the Arabs. He (peace be upon him) said: "For one of you to take his rope and go gather firewood on his back is better for him than to ask someone, who may give him or refuse him." This refers to what is obtained without effort, such as grass and firewood. And if a man were assumed to be cut off from people in the mountains, he would still have to go out to what the hills produce and what the high landmarks reveal, until he takes from that what sustains him. This is the meaning of his (peace be upon him) words: "If you were to rely upon Allah with the reliance due to Him, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out hungry in the morning and return full in the evening." So their going out and their returning is a cause. Therefore, how strange, how very strange, is the one who claims detachment and reliance on Allah in reality, yet sits at the crossroads of the path, abandons the straight path and the clear, upright method! In al-Bukhari, Ibn 'Abbas said: "The people of Yemen used to perform Hajj without taking provisions, saying, 'We are the reliant ones (al-mutawakkilun).' When they arrived, they asked people for food. Then Allah revealed: ﴿And take provisions﴾." It is not reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions (may Allah's good pleasure be upon them) that they set out on their journeys without provisions, and they were truly the reliant ones. Tawakkul (trust in Allah, reliance) is the heart's dependence on the Lord to set right one's affairs and gather one's needs for him, and then to take up the causes, merely by command. This is the truth. A man asked Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal: "I want to perform Hajj on the foot of tawakkul." He said: "Go out alone." He said: "No, only with people." He said to him: "Then you are depending on their camels." We have addressed this subject in the book "Qam' al-Hirs bi'l-Zuhd wa'l-Qana'ah wa Radd Dhull al-Su'al bi'l-Kutub wa'l-Shafa'ah."

**Question 4:** Muslim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The most beloved of lands to Allah are its mosques, and the most hated of lands to Allah are its markets." Al-Bazzar transmitted from Salman al-Farisi, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not be, if you can avoid it, the first to enter the market, nor the last to leave it, for it is the battlefield of Satan, and there he plants his banner." Abu Bakr al-Barqani transmitted it with a chain (musnadan) from Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Ghani, through the narration of 'Asim, from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, from Salman, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not be the first to enter the market, nor the last to leave it, for there Satan has laid his eggs and hatched them." So in these hadiths there is an indication of the disliked nature of entering the markets, especially in these times when men mix with women. Thus our scholars said, when falsehood became abundant in the markets and wrongdoing appeared in them: entering them is disliked for people of virtue and for those who are followed in religion, to keep them far from places where Allah is disobeyed. Therefore it is necessary for whoever Allah has tried with the market to keep in mind that he has entered the place of Satan and the place of his soldiers, and that if he stays there he will be ruined. Whoever is in this condition should limit himself to the degree of his necessity and guard himself against its evil consequences and its trial.

**The fifth matter:** The Prophet's (ﷺ) comparison of the marketplace to the battlefield is a fine comparison. The battlefield (*ma'raka*) is the place of fighting, so called because brave warriors clash there and wrestle one another. He likened the marketplace, and the Devil's activity there and his gaining power over people, to it, through the deception, trickery, and laxity in corrupt sales, lying, false oaths, the mingling of voices, and other things that bring people down, just as the battlefield brings down those who are struck down in it.

**The sixth matter:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for eating food, it is a necessity of creation, and there is no shame or blame (*dark*, meaning responsibility) in it. As for marketplaces, I heard the elders (*mashyakha*) of the people of knowledge say: "One should enter only the market of books and weapons." In my view, a person may enter every market for the need he has of it, but he should not eat there, because that brings down manliness and destroys dignity. Among the fabricated hadiths (*ahadith mawdu'a*) is: "Eating in the market is baseness." [The hadith is narrated by al-Tabarani from Abu Umama and by al-Khatib from Abu Hurayra, and al-Suyuti weakened it.]

I say: What the elders of the people of knowledge mentioned is good indeed, for that is free from looking at women and mixing with them, since that is not part of their needs. As for other markets, they are crowded with women, and shamelessness has overcome them, to the extent that you see a woman sitting in the *qaysariyyat* (covered markets) and elsewhere, displaying her adornment. This is a widespread evil in our time. We seek refuge in Allah from His wrath.

**The seventh matter:** Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated in his *Musnad*: Hammad ibn Zayd told us, saying: Amr ibn Dinar, steward (*qahraman*, meaning one who guards and manages what is under his hand, a Persian term) of the family of al-Zubayr, told us, from Salim, from his father, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "Whoever enters one of these markets and says: 'There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs dominion, and to Him belongs praise. He gives life and causes death, and He is living and does not die. In His hand is all good, and He is capable of all things,' Allah will record for him a thousand thousand good deeds, erase from him a thousand thousand sins, and build for him a palace in Paradise." It was also narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who added after "and erase from him a thousand thousand sins": "and raise for him a thousand thousand degrees, and build for him a house in Paradise." He said: This is a *gharib* (rare) hadith.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: This applies when he does not intend by that place anyone other than Allah (*siwahu*, meaning other than Allah, may He be exalted), so that he may populate it with obedience, since it was populated with disobedience, and adorn it with remembrance, since it was left idle by heedlessness, and so that he may teach the ignorant and remind the forgetful.

**The eighth matter:** Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient?﴾ That is: this world is a house of trial and testing. Allah, glorified is He, willed to make some of His servants a trial for others in general, among all people, believer and disbeliever. So the healthy person is a trial for the sick, the rich is a trial for the poor, and the patient poor is a trial for the rich. The meaning of this is that each one is tested by his companion. The rich is tested by the poor: he must support him and not mock him. The poor is tested by the rich: he must not envy him, and he should not take from him except what he gives him, and each of them should be patient in the truth. As al-Dahhak said regarding the meaning of "Will you be patient?": that is, in the truth.

Those afflicted with calamities say: "Why were we not granted health?" The blind man says: "Why was I not made like the one who sees?" And so is the case with everyone who has an affliction. The Messenger, who was singled out with the honour of prophethood, was a trial for the noble people among the disbelievers of his time. Likewise the scholars and just rulers. Do you not see their saying: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?" (Q. 43:31). So the trial is that the afflicted envies the healthy one, and patience is that each of them restrains himself: this one from insolence, and that one from impatience.

"Will you be patient?" has an omitted response, meaning "or will you not be patient?" It requires an answer, as al-Muzani said. Poverty drove him out, and he saw a eunuch in fine mounts and fine shoulders (i.e., luxurious conveyances and bearing), and something occurred to his mind; then he heard someone recite the verse "Will you be patient?" and he said: "Yes, our Lord! We will be patient and seek reward."

Ibn al-Qasim, the companion of Malik, recited this verse when he saw Ashhab ibn Abd al-Aziz passing by him in his domain, then he answered himself by saying: "We will be patient."

It is narrated from Abu al-Darda' that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Woe to the scholar from the ignorant, woe to the ignorant from the scholar, woe to the owner from the slave, woe to the slave from the owner, woe to the strong from the weak, woe to the weak from the strong, woe to the ruler from the subjects, and woe to the subjects from the ruler, and some of them are a trial for others." This is His saying: "And We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient?" It was transmitted by al-Tha'labi, may Allah cover him with His mercy.

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-As ibn Wa'il, Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, Utba ibn Rabi'a, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, when they saw Abu Dharr, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Ammar, Bilal, Suhayb, Amir ibn Fuhayra, Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, Mahja' the freed slave of Umar ibn al-Khattab, Jabr the freed slave of al-Hadrami, and their likes, and they said mockingly: "Shall we become Muslims and be like these?" Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed, addressing these believers: "Will you be patient?" regarding what you see of this harsh condition and poverty. So the address "Will you be patient?" is specific to the sincere believers (*al-muhaqqiqin*) of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is as if He made the respite given to the disbelievers and their being granted abundance a trial for the believers, that is, a test for them. When the Muslims were patient, Allah revealed concerning them: "Indeed I have rewarded them today for what they endured with patience" (Q. 23:111).

**The ninth matter:** Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾, that is, of every person, of whoever is patient or impatient, of whoever believes and whoever does not believe, and of whoever fulfils what is due upon him of the truth and whoever does not. It was also said: "Will you be patient?" means "Be patient!" Like "So will you desist?" (Q. 5:91), meaning "Desist!" Thus it is a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 21–22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who do not expect a meeting with Us said﴾. He means: those who do not fear the Resurrection and the meeting with Allah, that is, they do not believe in it. He said:

"When the bees sting, he does not hope for their sting, and he is at odds with them in a house of dense, busy woven hives."
[The verse is by Abu Dhu'ayb, and its explanation was given earlier in vol. 8, p. 311, of the first or second edition.]

It is also said: "do not expect" means "do not care." He said:

"By your life, when I am a Muslim, I do not hope, on whatever side I fall, that my death is in the way of Allah."
[The verse is from a qasidah of Khubayb ibn 'Adi, which he recited when he learned that the disbelievers had gathered to crucify him.]

Ibn Shajar: "do not hope" means "do not aspire." He said:

"Does a nation that killed Husayn hope for the intercession of his grandfather on the Day of Reckoning?"

﴿Why are the angels not sent down upon us﴾, that is, why were the angels not sent down, ﴿or do we not see our Lord﴾ directly, so that He would inform us of His messenger's mission? A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth..."﴾ up to His saying: ﴿"or you bring Allah and the angels as a guarantee."﴾ Allah said: ﴿They have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression﴾, since they asked of Allah an outrageous thing, because the angels are not seen except at death or at the descent of punishment, and Allah, exalted is He, cannot be perceived by sight, while He perceives sight, so no eye can see Him. Muqatil said: "transgressed" means "exalted themselves on earth." Al-'Utuww is the most extreme disbelief and the most vile wrongdoing. And if they are not satisfied with the miracles and this Qur'an, how would they be satisfied with angels? They cannot distinguish between them and the devils, and there must be a miracle for them, established by one who claims to be an angel; and the people have no right to demand a miracle after they have witnessed his miracle. As for His saying: ﴿On the day they see the angels, there will be no good news that day for the criminals﴾, it means that no one sees the angels except at death, when they give good news to the believers of Paradise and strike the polytheists and disbelievers with iron maces until their souls come out.

﴿And they will say, "A forbidding, forbidden [barrier]"﴾. It means the angels say: forbidden and prohibited is it that anyone enter Paradise except one who said "There is no god but Allah" and upheld its laws, according to Ibn 'Abbas and others. It is also said that this will be on the Day of Resurrection, as said by Mujahid and 'Atiyya al-'Awfi. 'Atiyya said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, the believer will be met with good news, but when the disbeliever sees that, he wishes for it, yet he does not see it from the angels." **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 25, verses 23–24:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make it scattered dust﴾. This is a warning about the great worth of the Day of Resurrection. That is, We intended by it what the criminals used to do of deeds of righteousness in their own estimation. It is said: "So-and-so turned to (qadima) a matter," meaning he intended it. Mujahid said: "qadimna" means "we intended." The rajiz (rhymed-verse poet) said:

*"The misguided Kharijites came upon (qadima) the servants of their Lord and said:*
*'Your blood is lawful to us.'"*

It is also said that this is the arrival (qudum) of the angels, and the act is attributed to Allah, Exalted is He, because it is by His command [[As in the original text. Ibn 'Atiyyah's wording is: "He attributed it to Himself because it was by His command."]].

(﴿and made it scattered dust﴾) That is, it will not benefit them. That is, We nullified it through disbelief. The word *habaa'* (dust) is not from the roots with a hamza; the hamza was added because of the meeting of two sukun letters (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). Its diminutive is *Hubayy*, in the place of nominative case (*raf'*). Some grammarians say: *Hubay* in the place of nominative case, related by al-Nahhas [[Al-Nahhas said: "The estimate according to him is *hubay*."]]. Its singular is *habaah*, and its plural is *ahbaa'*. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said, describing a she-camel:

*"You see behind her, from the sound of her hooves and the fall of her feet,*
*a fine dust like ahbaa'."*

[[His saying "behind her" means behind the she-camel. *Al-rajʿ* is the sound of her legs; *al-waqʿ* is the sound of her hooves; *al-manin* is the fine dust that she raises.]]

Al-Harith related from 'Ali that he said: "*Al-habaa' al-manthur* is the sunlight that enters through a window." Al-Azhari said: "*Al-habaa'* is what comes out through a window in the light of the sun, resembling dust." Its interpretation: Allah, Exalted is He, nullified their deeds until they became like scattered *habaa'*. As for *al-habaa' al-munbathth*, it is what horses raise with their hooves of dust. *Al-munbathth* means scattered. Ibn 'Arafa said: "*Al-habwah* and *al-habaa'* are fine dust." Al-Jawhari said: "It is said of it, when it rises, *haba yahbu hawban*, and I *ahbaytuhu*. *Al-habwah* is dust." Ru'bah said:

*"Its landmarks appear to us after the drowning in the cutting of the mirage and the dust-clouds of fine dust."*

[[*Al-daqiq* is what is finely ground of earth; its singular is *al-daqaa*, as you say *al-julaa* and *al-jullu*.]]

A place is said to be *habi al-turab*, meaning its dust is like *habaa'* in fineness. It is also said that it is what the winds scatter of dry leaves of trees; this was said by Qatadah and Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is water poured out. It is also said that it is ashes; this was said by Ubayd ibn Ya'la [[As in the original text. In *Ruh al-Ma'ani* it reads: Ya'la ibn Ubayd.]].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day will be better in their resting place and finer in their resting-place at midday﴾. The discussion of this has already been mentioned at His saying: ﴿Say: Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which has been promised to the righteous?﴾ [[See p. 9 of this part.]]

Al-Nahhas said: The Kufans permit "honey is sweeter than vinegar," and this is a rejected view, because the meaning of "so-and-so is better than so-and-so" is that he has more good than the other, and there is no sweetness in vinegar. It is not permissible to say: "The Christian is better than the Jew," because there is no good in either of them, so that one of them would have more good. Rather, it is said: "The Jew is worse than the Christian." According to this, it is the usage of the Arabs. *Mustaqarran* (in abode) is in the accusative as an adverb of place if it is parsed outside the pattern of *af'alu minka* (the comparative form). The meaning is: they have good in an abode. If it is of the pattern of *af'alu minka*, its accusative is as a specification (*tamyiz*), as al-Nahhas and al-Mahdawi said.

Qatadah said: ﴿and finer in resting-place﴾ means a dwelling and a place of refuge. It is also said that it is according to what the Arabs know of the midday rest (*maqil nisf al-nahar*). From this is the hadith, traced to the Prophet: "Allah, blessed and exalted, will finish the reckoning of the creation in the span of half a day, and the people of Paradise and the people of Hellfire will take their midday rest in the Fire." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "The midday of the Day of Resurrection will not reach its half until these people arrive in Paradise and those in the Fire," reciting: ﴿Then indeed their resting place is toward the Blazing Fire﴾, as it is in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The reckoning begins from the beginning of that Day, so the day of Resurrection does not reach its midpoint until the people of Paradise are said to be in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire. From this is what is narrated: "Take a midday rest (*qilu*), for the devils do not take a midday rest."

Qasim ibn Asbagh mentioned, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On a day whose measure is fifty thousand years." I said: "How long this day is!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, it will be made light for the believer until it is lighter for him than the obligatory prayer that he prays in the world."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 25–26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the day the sky will be split open with the clouds﴾, meaning: and remember the day the sky is split open with the clouds. ʿĀṣim, al-Aʿmash, Yaḥyā, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Abū ʿAmr read "tashaqqaqu" with a light shīn, and its origin is "tatashaqqaqu" with two tāʾs, so the first is dropped for lightness (takhfīf). Abū ʿUbayd preferred this reading. The rest read "tashshaqqaqu" with a doubled shīn, through assimilation (idghām), and Abū Ḥātim preferred this. Likewise in Surah Qāf [[In His saying: "On the day the earth will be split open from them, swiftly..." (50:44)]]. "With the clouds" means "from the clouds." The bāʾ and ʿan (from) alternate, as you say: "I shot with the bow" and "I shot from the bow." It is related that the sky will be split open to release a white, thin cloud like a mist, and this was only for the Children of Israel in their wandering (tīh), so the sky will split open for it. This is what He, may He be exalted, referred to: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds?﴾ (2:210).

(﴿And the angels will be sent down﴾) from the heavens, and the Lord, mighty and majestic, will come in the eight who carry the Throne, to judge between people, in a manner that is fitting for Him to be described by, not in the manner in which the attributes of created beings are described, such as movement and displacement. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The lowest heaven will split open and its inhabitants will descend, and they will be more numerous than those on the earth of jinn and humankind. Then the second heaven will split open and its inhabitants will descend, and they will be more numerous than those of the lowest heaven. Then likewise until the seventh heaven splits open, and then the Karūbiyyūn [[al-Karūbiyyūn (with a fatḥah on the kāf): the chiefs of the angels, among them Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl and Isrāfīl, who are the closest (al-muqarrabūn). Al-karb means nearness.]] and the bearers of the Throne will descend. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And the angels will be sent down, a descent﴾, that is, from the sky to the earth, for the reckoning of the two weighty ones (humans and jinn). It was also said: the sky will split open with the cloud that is between it and people, and when the cloud splits, the sky splits; when the sky splits, its structure will be undone, it will be folded up, and the angels will be sent down to another place other than it. Ibn Kathīr read "wa-nunzila al-malāʾikata" with a fatḥah on the lām, from al-inzāl, and the rest read "wa-nuzzila al-malāʾikatu" with a ḍammah. Its evidence is "tanzīlan" (a descent); had it been the first, he would have said "inzālan." It has been said that "nunazzilu" and "anzala" have the same meaning, so "tanzīlan" comes in agreement with "nuzzila." ʿAbd al-Wahhāb related from Abū ʿAmr: "wa-nazzala al-malāʾikata tanzīlan." Ibn Masʿūd read "wa-unzila al-malāʾikatu." Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read: "wa-nuzzilat al-malāʾikatu." And it is related from him: "wa-tanazzalat al-malāʾikatu."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The dominion that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾. "Al-mulk" is the subject (mubtadaʾ), "al-ḥaqq" is its attribute (ṣifah), and "lil-Raḥmān" is the predicate (khabar), because the dominion that passes away and ends is not dominion. Thus on that day the dominions of the possessors of dominion are nullified, their claims are cut off, every king and his kingdom disappear, and the true dominion remains for Allah alone.

(﴿And it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾) meaning: because of the terrors that befall them and the disgrace and humiliation that overtake them. It is light for the believers, lighter than an obligatory prayer, as has preceded in the hadith. This verse indicates it, for if it is difficult for the disbelievers, then it is easy for the believers. It is said: ʿasura yaʿsuru, and ʿasira yaʿsaru.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verses 27–29:**

God's words: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer bites his hands﴾. The past tense is عَضِضْتُ. Al-Kisa'i reported عَضَضْتُ with a fatha on the first ḍād. Uqbah was killed by Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. He was among the captives at the Battle of Badr, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered his execution. He said, "Am I to be killed before them?" The Prophet ﷺ said, "Yes, for your disbelief and your insolence." He said, "Who will take care of the children?" The Prophet ﷺ said, "The Fire." Then Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up and killed him. Umayyah was killed by the Prophet ﷺ himself. This was one of the proofs of the prophethood of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, because he reported about the two of them this matter, and they were both killed in disbelief. They were not named in the verse, because that is more effective in conveying the lesson, so that it may be known that this is the path of every wrongdoer who follows others in disobedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and others said: Uqbah had intended to embrace Islam, but Ubayy ibn Khalaf prevented him, and they were close companions. The Prophet ﷺ killed them both: he killed Uqbah on the day of Badr by execution in cold blood, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf in single combat on the day of Uhud. This was related by al-Qushayri and al-Tha'labi, and the first account was related by al-Nahhas. Al-Suhayli said: "And the day the wrongdoer bites his hands" refers to Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, who was a friend of Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. It is also narrated that Ubayy ibn Khalaf was the brother of Umayyah. Uqbah had prepared a banquet and invited the Quraysh, and he invited the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but he refused to come unless Uqbah embraced Islam. Uqbah disliked that any of the nobles of the Quraysh should stay away from his food, so he embraced Islam and uttered the two testimonies. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to him and ate from his food. His friend Umayyah ibn Khalaf, or Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who had been absent, reproached him. Uqbah said: "I saw it as a great matter that a man of the nobles of the Quraysh should not come to my food." His friend said to him: "I will not be content until you go back and spit in his face, trample his neck, and say such-and-such." So the enemy of Allah did what his friend had commanded him, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer bites his hands﴾. Al-Dahhak said: When Uqbah spat in the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his spittle came back onto his own face, scorching his face and lips, until it left a mark on his face and burned both his cheeks. That mark remained on his face until he was killed. His biting of his hands is the action of a regretful, grieving person because of his obedience to his friend.

﴿He says: "Oh, would that I had taken a way together with the Messenger."﴾ In this world, meaning a path to Paradise.

﴿"Oh woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a friend."﴾ This is a call of woe and perdition upon himself for allying with and following the disbeliever.

﴿"Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a friend."﴾ He means Umayyah. He was referred to by an epithet and not named explicitly, so that this threat would not be restricted to him alone, but would encompass everyone who does the like of their deeds. Mujahid and Abu Raja said: "The wrongdoer" is general, applying to every wrongdoer, and "so-and-so" is Satan. The proponent of this view argued from what follows: ﴿And Satan is ever a deserter to man﴾.

Al-Hasan recited يَا وَيْلَتِي (Ya Wailati). Its explanation has already been given at Hud. The khalil (close friend) is the companion and intimate, and its explanation has already been given at al-Nisa.

﴿He has led me astray from the Reminder﴾. That is, this regretful one says: "He has led me astray, the one I took as a friend in this world, away from the Qur'an and faith in it." It is also said that "the Reminder" means the Messenger.

﴿And Satan is ever a deserter to man﴾. It has been said that this is the words of God and not the words of the wrongdoer. The completion of the speech according to this view is at His words: "after it had come to me." Khadhl means abandonment of help, and from it comes the desertion of Iblis of the polytheists when Suraqah ibn Malik appeared, and when he saw the angels he disowned them. Whoever turns others away from the path of Allah and is obeyed in disobedience to Allah is a satan to man, a deserter at the descent of punishment and trial. How well said is the one who said:

Avoid the evil companion and cut his ties;
if you cannot escape him, then tolerate him.
Love the loved one of truthfulness, and beware of his disputing;
you will obtain from him the pure affection, so long as you do not argue with him.
In gray hair there is what restrains the forbearing from youthful folly,
when its fires have flared up on his cheek.

Another said:

Keep company with the best of people wherever you meet them;
the best companion is the one who is chaste.
People are like dirhams that you weigh,
and among them you find silver and counterfeit.

In the Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Musa, the Prophet ﷺ said: "The likeness of the righteous companion and the evil companion is like the carrier of musk and the blower of the bellows. The carrier of musk will either give you some, or you will buy from him, or you will get a pleasant scent from him. The blower of the bellows will either burn your clothes, or you will get a foul smell from him." This is the wording of Muslim. Abu Dawud also related it from the hadith of Anas.

Abu Bakr al-Bazzar related from Ibn Abbas that he said: It was said, "O Messenger of Allah, which of our companions is best?" He said: "Whoever reminds you of Allah by seeing him, whose speech increases your knowledge, and whose deeds remind you of the Hereafter."

Malik ibn Dinar said: If you carry stones with the righteous, that is better for you than eating sweetmeat (khabis) with the wicked. Khabis is a sweet made from dates and ghee.

He recited:

Keep company with the best of people, and you will be safe and secure;
keep company with the worst of people, and one day you will regret it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verses 30–31:

His saying, Exalted is He: (And the Messenger said, "My Lord, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned." [This refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), who complains to Allah, Exalted is He.]

(Indeed, my people have taken this Qur'an as abandoned.) That is, they spoke about it other than the truth, saying that it is sorcery and poetry. This is related from Mujahid and al-Nakha'i. It was also said that the meaning of "mahjur" (abandoned) is "matruk" (left aside). So Allah, blessed and exalted, consoled him and comforted him with His saying: (And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals.) That is: just as We have appointed for you, O Muhammad, an enemy from among the polytheists of your people, who, according to Ibn Abbas, was Abu Jahl, so too have We appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the polytheists of his people. So be patient in obedience to My command as they were patient, for I will guide you and support you against everyone who opposes you. It has also been said that the Messenger's saying "My Lord" is said on the Day of Resurrection, meaning: they abandoned the Qur'an and abandoned me and denied me. Anas said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever learns the Qur'an and teaches it, and hangs its copy [[In the original text: "whoever learns the Qur'an, teaches it, and hangs its copy..." The correctness of this report is discussed in Ruh al-Ma'ani, al-Baydawi and al-Shihab, since its chain includes Abu Hadba, who was a liar.]] and does not attend to it, nor reflect upon it, will come on the Day of Resurrection clinging to it, saying: 'O Lord of the worlds, indeed this servant of Yours took me as abandoned, so judge between me and him.'" Al-Tha'labi related it.

(And your Lord suffices as a guide and a helper.) This is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) or as a specification (tamyiz), meaning: He will guide you and support you, so do not care about whoever opposes you. Ibn Abbas said: The enemy of the Prophet (ﷺ) was Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him.
