The verse, "And those who disbelieve say, 'Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?'"

There is a difference of opinion about who said this, on two views. The first is that they were the disbelievers of Quraysh, as reported by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that they were the Jews, when they saw the Qur'an being revealed in parts, and said: "Why was it not sent down to him all at once, as the Torah was sent down to Musa, the Gospel to 'Isa, and the Psalms [to Dawud]?" [[An addition required by the context.]] Allah the Exalted said: "Thus" (that is, We did so) "that We may strengthen your heart by it" (We strengthen your heart by it, so that you may understand it and bear it). This is because the earlier scriptures were sent down to prophets who could write and read, whereas the Qur'an was sent down to an unlettered Prophet. Also, the Qur'an contains the abrogating (nasikh) and the abrogated (mansukh) [verses], and some of it is an answer to those who asked about particular matters. So We divided it so that it would be better retained by the Prophet (ﷺ) and easier for the one who acts upon it. Thus, whenever a new revelation descended, it increased his heart in strength.

I say: If it is asked, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down in a single go, and why did He not memorise it for him, since that was within His power?" The answer is: it is within the power of Allah to teach him the Book and the Qur'an in a single instant, but He did not do so, and no one can object to His judgement. We have already explained the wisdom behind this.

It has also been said that His words "Thus" are part of the speech of the polytheists, meaning: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once, thus," that is, like the Torah and the Gospel. In that case the pause falls on "Thus," and then the next words begin: "that We may strengthen your heart by it." It is also possible that the pause falls on His words "all at once," and then the next words begin: "Thus, that We may strengthen your heart by it," meaning: "We sent it down to you thus, in parts, that We may strengthen your heart by it."

Ibn al-Anbari said: The first view is better and finer, and the second view is also supported by an exegetical report (tafsir). Muhammad ibn 'Uthman al-Shaybi related to us, saying: Minjab related to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara related to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: "Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree" [[See vol. 20, p. 129.]]: "He said: The Qur'an was sent down all at once from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to the Preserved Tablet, and then to the noble scribes in the heaven. Then the noble scribes revealed it to Jibril in portions over twenty nights, and Jibril, upon him be peace, revealed it to Muhammad over twenty years." He said: This is His words: "So I swear by the positions of the stars" [[See vol. 17, p. 223.]], meaning the stars of the Qur'an, "and indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew. Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an." He said: When it was not sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ) all at once, those who disbelieved said: "Why was it not sent down to him all at once?" So Allah, blessed and exalted, said: "Thus, that We may strengthen your heart by it," O Muhammad.

"And We have recited it in measured recitation" (wa rattalnahu tartilan): he says: "We have made it gradual, a little after a little."

"And they do not bring you any example except that We bring you the truth and the best explanation" (ahsana tafsiran). He says: Had We sent down the Qur'an all at once and then they asked you, you would not have had an answer to give. But We hold it back from you, and when they ask you, you answer. Al-Nahhas said: This was one of the signs of prophethood, for they never asked about anything without being answered, and this cannot happen except through a prophet. This was therefore a strengthening of his heart and of theirs. This is supported by His words: "And they do not bring you any example except that We bring you the truth and the best explanation." Had it been sent down all at once, with the obligations contained in it, it would have been burdensome for them. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, knew that the good lay in sending it down in parts, because they were admonished by it time after time. Had it been sent down in one go, the sense of admonition would have ceased. Moreover, there is abrogation and abrogated [material] in it, and they worshipped by means of a ruling until a specific time that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, knew to be good, after which the abrogation descended. It would be impossible for it to descend all at once saying: "Do this and do not do that."

Al-Nahhas said: The better view is that the pause should fall on "all at once," because if one pauses on "Thus," the meaning becomes "like the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms," and no prior mention of them has been made.

Al-Dahhak said: "And the best explanation" means the best detailed account. The meaning is: better than their example in detail. The second part is omitted because the hearer knows it.

It has also been said: The polytheists used to seek help from the People of the Book, and distortion (tahrif) and alteration (tabdil) had overtaken the People of the Book. So what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought was a better explanation than what they had, because they used to mix the truth with falsehood, and pure truth is better than truth mixed with falsehood. For this reason He said: "And do not mix the truth with falsehood" [[See vol. 1, p. 364 onwards.]].

It has also been said: "They do not bring you any example" refers to their statement about the attribute of 'Isa, that he was created without a father, "except that We bring you the truth", that is, with that which refutes their argument, like Adam, who was created without a father or mother.

The verse, "And those who disbelieve say, 'Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?'"

There is a difference of opinion about who said this, on two views. The first is that they were the disbelievers of Quraysh, as reported by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that they were the Jews, when they saw the Qur'an being revealed in parts, and said: "Why was it not sent down to him all at once, as the Torah was sent down to Musa, the Gospel to 'Isa, and the Psalms [to Dawud]?" [[An addition required by the context.]] Allah the Exalted said: "Thus" (that is, We did so) "that We may strengthen your heart by it" (We strengthen your heart by it, so that you may understand it and bear it). This is because the earlier scriptures were sent down to prophets who could write and read, whereas the Qur'an was sent down to an unlettered Prophet. Also, the Qur'an contains the abrogating (nasikh) and the abrogated (mansukh) [verses], and some of it is an answer to those who asked about particular matters. So We divided it so that it would be better retained by the Prophet (ﷺ) and easier for the one who acts upon it. Thus, whenever a new revelation descended, it increased his heart in strength.

I say: If it is asked, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down in a single go, and why did He not memorise it for him, since that was within His power?" The answer is: it is within the power of Allah to teach him the Book and the Qur'an in a single instant, but He did not do so, and no one can object to His judgement. We have already explained the wisdom behind this.

It has also been said that His words "Thus" are part of the speech of the polytheists, meaning: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once, thus," that is, like the Torah and the Gospel. In that case the pause falls on "Thus," and then the next words begin: "that We may strengthen your heart by it." It is also possible that the pause falls on His words "all at once," and then the next words begin: "Thus, that We may strengthen your heart by it," meaning: "We sent it down to you thus, in parts, that We may strengthen your heart by it."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those who will be gathered on their faces to Hell﴾. This was discussed earlier in (Surat) "Subhan" [see vol. 10, p. 333].

(﴿Those are worse in position﴾) because they are in Hell. Muqatil said: The disbelievers said to the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ): "He is the worst of creation." So this verse was revealed.

(﴿And further astray in way﴾) i.e., in religion and path. The construction of the verse is: "And they do not bring you any example except that We bring you the truth, while you are victorious over them with clear proofs, and they are being gathered on their faces."

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 25, verses 35–36:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book﴾. He means the Tawrat (Torah).

(﴿And We made his brother Harun a minister with him﴾). It was discussed in "Ta-Ha" [[See vol. 11, p. 191 and p. 12.]]. (﴿So We said: Go, both of you﴾). The address is to both of them. It was also said that Musa (ﷺ) was in fact commanded to go alone, in meaning. This is like His words: ﴿they forgot their fish﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 161.]], and His words: ﴿From both of them emerge pearl and coral﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 333.]], when it emerges from only one of them. Al-Nahhas said: This is something one should not presume to say about the Book of Allah, the Exalted, when He, Mighty and Majestic, has said: ﴿Speak to him gently, perhaps he may take heed or fear. They said: Our Lord, we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress. He said: Do not fear; indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing. So go to him and say: I am the messenger of your Lord.﴾

A parallel to this is ﴿and below them are two gardens﴾. And He, Mighty is His praise, said: ﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs﴾. Al-Qushayri said: His words in another place, ﴿Go to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed﴾, do not contradict this, because when the two were commanded, each one of them was commanded. It is also possible to say that Musa was commanded first, and then, when he said, ﴿and appoint for me a minister from my family﴾, He said: ﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh﴾.

(﴿to the people who denied Our signs﴾). He means Pharaoh, Haman and the Qibt (Copts).

(﴿Then We destroyed them﴾). In the speech there is an implied element, meaning: so they denied the two of them. (﴿Then We utterly destroyed them﴾), meaning: We annihilated them with annihilation.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 37:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the people of Noah﴾. Regarding the case-ending (naṣb) of "qawma" (qawma), there are four opinions. The first: it is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the pronoun of "fa-dammarnāhum" (the hā' and mīm). The second: it is in the sense of "remember" (udhkur). The third: it is by implying a verb which is explained by what follows it, and the estimated meaning is: "And We drowned the people of Noah, We drowned them." The fourth: it is governed by "aghraqnāhum" (We drowned them), as said by al-Farrāʾ. Al-Naḥḥās (al-Nahhas) rejected this, saying: because "aghraqnā" is not one of the verbs that take two objects, so that it would govern both the pronoun and "qawma Nūḥ".

(﴿When they denied the messengers﴾) The mention is of the category (jins), while what is meant is Noah alone, because at that time there was no messenger sent to them except Noah alone. Noah was sent only with "there is no god but Allah" and with belief in what Allah sends down. So when they denied him, that was a denial of everyone sent after him with this same declaration. It has also been said: whoever denies one messenger has denied all the messengers, because they are not distinguished from one another in faith, and because there is no prophet who does not confirm the other prophets of Allah; so whoever denies one prophet among them has denied every prophet who confirmed him.

(﴿We drowned them﴾) That is, by the flood, as mentioned previously in Surah Hud.

(﴿And We made them a sign for mankind﴾) That is, a manifest sign of Our power. (﴿And We have prepared for the wrongdoers﴾) That is, the polytheists among the people of Noah, (﴿a painful punishment﴾) That is, in the Hereafter. It has also been said: that is, this is My way with every wrongdoer.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 38:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And ʿAd and Thamud and the companions of the Rass, and generations between that, many﴾. All of this is in apposition (*maʿtūf*) to "the people of Noah" if "the people of Noah" is in the accusative by apposition, or in the sense of "remember." It may also be in the accusative as coordinated with the pronoun in "fadammarnāhum" (We destroyed them), or with the pronoun in "jaʿalnāhum" (We made them). This is the view chosen by al-Nahhas, because it is closer to it. It may also be in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "Remember ʿAd, who denied Hud, so Allah destroyed them with the barren wind, and Thamud, who denied Salih, so they were destroyed by the shout (*al-rajfa*)."

"Companions of the Rass": in the speech of the Arabs, *al-Rass* is the well that is not lined with stone (*ghayr maṭwiyya*). Its plural is *risas*. The poet said [[He is al-Nabigha al-Ja'di. Al-tanabila: short men.]]:

*Tanabila yahfirūna al-risās* ... meaning: wells of the mines.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "I asked Kaʿb about the companions of the Rass, and he said: 'The companion of Ya-Sin, who said: "O my people, follow the messengers" [[See vol. 15, p. 17 onward.]], was killed by his people, who threw him into a well of theirs called al-Rass.'" Muqatil said the same. Al-Suddi said: They are the people of the story of Ya-Sin, the people of Antioch, and al-Rass is a well in Antioch in which they killed Habib al-Najjar, the believer of the family of Ya-Sin, so they were named after it.

ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: They were a people who worshipped a pine tree, and their prophet, who was of the descendants of Judah, invoked a curse upon them, so the tree dried up. They killed him and threw him into a well, and a black cloud overshadowed them and burned them.

Ibn ʿAbbas also said: They are a people in Adharbayjan who killed prophets, so their trees and crops dried up, and they died of hunger and thirst.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: They were people of a well, sitting beside it, and they were owners of livestock. They worshipped idols. Allah sent Shuʿayb to them, but they denied him and harmed him, and they persisted in their disbelief and transgression. While they were around the well in their dwellings, it collapsed upon them and their homes, and Allah caused them to sink into the earth, so they all perished.

Qatada said: The companions of the Rass and the companions of al-Aykah (the thicket) were two nations to whom Allah sent Shuʿayb, and they denied him, so Allah punished them with two punishments. Qatada also said: al-Rass is a town in Falj al-Yamama.

ʿIkrima said: They are a people who buried their prophet alive in a well. The evidence for this is what Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi narrated from someone who told him that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first of mankind to enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection is a black slave. That is because Allah sent a prophet to his people, and none believed in him except that black slave. The people of the town dug a well and threw their prophet into it alive, and they closed it over him with a huge rock. The black slave used to gather firewood on his back and sell it, and bring him his food and drink. Allah helped him to lift that rock until he lowered it to him. One day, while he was gathering firewood, he slept, and Allah struck his ear with sleep for seven years. Then he awoke, stretched, and leaned on his other side, and Allah struck his ear for seven years again. Then he awoke, carried his bundle of firewood, sold it, and brought his food and drink to the well, but he did not find him. Allah had shown his people a sign, so they brought him out, believed in him, and believed him, and that prophet died."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "That black slave is indeed the first to enter Paradise."

Al-Mahdawi and al-Tha'labi also mentioned this report, and the wording is that of al-Tha'labi. He said: "These believed in their prophet, so it is not permissible that they be the companions of the Rass, because Allah informed us that He destroyed the companions of the Rass, unless they were destroyed for innovations they introduced after their prophet."

Al-Kalbi said: The companions of the Rass are a people to whom Allah sent a prophet, and they ate him. Their women were the first to practise *suhq* (lesbianism). This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

It was also said: They are the companions of the *Ukhdud* (the trench), who dug trenches and burned the believers in them, and this will come [[See vol. 19, p. 284.]].

It was also said: They are remnants of the people of Thamud, and that al-Rass is the well mentioned in *al-Hajj* in His saying: ﴿and a well abandoned﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 75.]], as has been previously stated.

In *al-Sihah* (the lexicon of al-Jawhari): "*Al-Rass* is the name of a well that belonged to a remnant of Thamud."

Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad said, from his father: The companions of the Rass were a people who considered *suhq* good for their women, and all their women were *sahhaqat* (practitioners of female homosexuality).

It is narrated from a hadith of Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the signs of the Hour is that men will be satisfied with men, and women with women, and that is *suhq*."

It was also said: al-Rass is water and palm trees belonging to the Banu Asad. It was also said: it is the snow piled up in the mountains, mentioned by al-Qushayri.

What we mentioned first is the well-known meaning, namely any excavation that is dug, such as a grave, a mine, or a well. Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-Rass* is every well that has not been lined, and its plural is *risas*. The poet said: *Wa-hum sa'irūna ila ardihim fa-ya layta-hum yahfirūna al-risas.* And *al-Rass* is the name of a valley in the saying of Zuhayr: *Bakarna bukūran wa-istaharna bi-suhratin fa-hunna li-wadi al-Rass ka-al-yadi lil-fam* (They came at dawn and went out at the pre-dawn, and they are to the valley of al-Rass like the hand to the mouth).

*Rassa* means: he dug a well. *Russa al-mayyit* means: the dead was buried. *Al-Rass* also means reconciling between people, and also corrupting them, and *rassastu baynahum* (I reconciled between them / I corrupted between them) is one of the words that have opposite meanings. It has been said regarding the companions of the Rass other than what we have mentioned; this was recorded by al-Tha'labi and others.

(And generations between that, many) means nations that none knows except Allah, between the people of Noah and ʿAd, and Thamud and the companions of the Rass.

It is narrated from al-Rabiʿ ibn Khaytham that he fell ill, and it was said to him: "Will you not seek treatment, for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has commanded it?" He said: "I had intended to do so, then I reflected within myself, and I found that ʿAd, Thamud, the companions of the Rass, and generations between that, many, were more numerous and more eager to gather wealth. There were physicians among them, yet neither the one who described (the illness) among them remained, nor the one who was described. So he refused to seek treatment, and he did not remain more than five days until he died. May Allah have mercy on him."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 39:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to each We set forth parables﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, "And We warned each [of them], to whom We set forth the parables, and We made the proof clear to them, and We did not set forth for them false parables as these disbelievers do." It was also said: it is in the accusative on the presumption of "We mentioned each" or the like, because the setting forth of parables is a reminder and admonition. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi. The meaning is one.

(﴿And each We destroyed with complete destruction﴾) That is, We destroyed them with punishment. And "tabbartu al-shay'" means I broke the thing. Al-Mu'arrij and al-Akhfash said: "We destroyed them with destruction" (dammarnahum tadmiran). The ta' and the ba' are substituted for the dal and the mim.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they have certainly passed by the town﴾ — meaning the idolaters of Makkah. "The town" is the town of the people of Lut. "Rain of evil" (matar al-su') refers to the stones with which they were rained upon.

(﴿Have they not been seeing it?﴾) — i.e., during their journeys, so that they might take heed. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Quraysh, in their trade to al-Sham, would pass by the cities of the people of Lut, as Allah, exalted is He, said: "And indeed you pass by them in the morning." 

And He said: "And indeed, they are on a road that remains." And this has been mentioned previously [see vol. 10, p. 45].

(﴿Rather, they did not expect a resurrection﴾) — i.e., they did not believe in the Resurrection. It is also possible that the meaning of "yarjuna" (expect) is "yakhafuna" (fear). It is also possible that it retains its own meaning, and then its meaning is: "Rather, they did not expect the reward of the Hereafter."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verses 41–42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they see you, they take you not except in mockery﴾. The answer (jawab) to "idha" (when) is "in yattakhidhunaka" (they take you), because its meaning is "yattakhidhunaka." It has also been said that the answer is omitted, and it is "qalu" (they say) or "yaqulun" (they say): "Is this the one whom..." and his saying "in yattakhidhunaka illa huzuwan" is a parenthetical statement (kalam mu'tarid). It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, who used to say to the Prophet ﷺ in mockery: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?" The returning pronoun (al-a'id) is omitted, meaning "whom Allah has sent (ba'athahu)." "Rasulan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and the sense is: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger (mursalan)?" "Ahadha" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "alladhi" is its predicate (khabar). "Rasulan" is in the accusative as a state (hal). "Ba'atha" is in the relative clause (silat) of "alladhi," and the name of Allah, mighty and majestic, is the agent of "ba'atha." It is permissible that it be a verbal noun (masdar), because the meaning of "ba'atha" is "arsala" (sent), and the meaning of "rasulan" in this case would be "risalatan" (a mission). The alif is for interrogation in the sense of affirmation (taqrir) and belittlement (ihtiqar).

﴿In kada la-yudillana﴾, meaning: they said, "He had almost led us astray..."

﴿'an alihatina law la an sabarna 'alayha﴾, meaning: we would have restrained ourselves in worshipping them. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in way﴾.

He means: who is further astray in religion, they or Muhammad? And they saw it on the day of Badr.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verses 41–42:

The returning pronoun (al-a'id) is omitted, meaning "whom Allah has sent (ba'athahu)." "Rasulan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and the sense is: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger (mursalan)?" "Ahadha" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "alladhi" is its predicate (khabar). "Rasulan" is in the accusative as a state (hal). "Ba'atha" is in the relative clause (silat) of "alladhi," and the name of Allah, mighty and majestic, is the agent of "ba'atha." It is permissible that it be a verbal noun (masdar), because the meaning of "ba'atha" is "arsala" (sent), and the meaning of "rasulan" in this case would be "risalatan" (a mission). The alif is for interrogation in the sense of affirmation (taqrir) and belittlement (ihtiqar).

﴿In kada la-yudillana﴾, meaning: they said, "He had almost led us astray..."

﴿'an alihatina law la an sabarna 'alayha﴾, meaning: we would have restrained ourselves in worshipping them. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in way﴾.

He means: who is further astray in religion, they or Muhammad? And they saw it on the day of Badr.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 43:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you seen him who takes his own desire as his god?﴾ He (Allah) astonished His Prophet ﷺ at their persistence in polytheism and their obstinacy in it, despite their acknowledgement that He is their Creator and their Provider, and yet a man deliberately goes to a stone and worships it without any proof.

Al-Kalbi and others said: When a man among the Arabs came to desire something, he would worship it besides Allah; and when he saw something better than it, he would abandon the first and worship the better one. Accordingly, the meaning is: "Have you seen him who takes his god by his desire," so the preposition has been omitted.

Ibn Abbas said: "Desire (hawa) is a god worshipped besides Allah," and then he recited this verse.

The poet said:

By the life of her father, if she were to show herself to an ascetic who had withdrawn from the world into one of the rites of worship,
He would pray to her before prayer to his Lord, and he would not turn back in this world from the deeds of a murderous woman.

It has also been said: "Takes his god as his desire" means he obeys his desire. It is narrated from al-Hasan: "He does not desire anything except that he follows it," and the meaning is one.

﴿Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ That is, a protector and a guarantor, so that you could bring him back to faith and take him out of this corruption. That is, guidance and misguidance are not entrusted to your will; rather, your duty is only to convey the message. This is a refutation of the Qadariyya. Then it was said: it has been abrogated by the verse of fighting. It was also said: it has not been abrogated, because the verse is a consolation for the Prophet ﷺ.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 44:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do you suppose that most of them hear or understand?﴾ He did not say "that they," because among them are those who He knew would believe. And Allah, mighty and majestic, censured them by this. "Or do you suppose that most of them hear" a hearing of acceptance, "or reflect on what you say so that they understand it?" That is, they are in the position of one who neither understands nor hears. It was also said: the meaning is that since they did not benefit from what they heard, it is as though they had not heard, and the intended people are the people of Mecca. It was also said: "am" (or) here carries the meaning of "bal" (rather) in such a place.

(﴿They are only like cattle﴾) That is, in eating and drinking, not reflecting on the Hereafter.

(﴿Rather, they are more astray﴾) Since there is no reckoning and no punishment for cattle. Muqatil said: The beasts know their Lord, are guided to their pastures, and submit to their owners who look after them, whereas these do not submit and do not know their Lord who created them and provided for them. It was also said: because if beasts do not understand the soundness of monotheism and prophethood, they do not believe in their falsehood either.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verses 45–46:

Allah's statement: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord extends the shade?﴾ This seeing may be visual sight, and it may be knowledge. Al-Hasan and others said: "The extension of the shade is from the break of dawn until the sunrise." It was also said: "It is from the sun's disappearance until its rising." The first view is more correct. The evidence for this is that there is no hour better than that hour, for in it the sick person finds relief, and so does the traveler and everyone who has an ailment. In it the souls of the dead, and their spirits, return to their bodies, and the souls of the living are refreshed. This quality is absent after sunset. Abu al-'Aliyah said: "The day of Paradise is like this," and he pointed to the hour of the worshippers who pray the dawn prayer.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Al-zill (shade) is in the morning, and al-fay' (shadow) is in the evening, because it returns after the sun has passed its zenith. It is called fay' because it turns (faa'a) from the east toward the west." The poet, who is Humayd ibn Thawr, describing a sarhah (a large tree under which one takes shelter, not one grazed by animals), and using it as a metaphor for a woman, said:

"Neither the shade can withstand it from the coolness of the forenoon,
nor does the shadow taste of the coolness of the evening."

Ibn al-Sikkit said: "Al-zill is what the sun has removed, and al-fay' is what has removed the sun." Abu 'Ubaydah related from Ru'bah, who said: "Everything on which the sun was and then left it is fay'; and everything on which the sun has not been is zill."

﴿And if He had willed, He would have made it still﴾, that is, permanent and fixed, never removed by the sun. Ibn 'Abbas said: "He means until the Day of Resurrection." It was also said: "The meaning is that if He had willed, He would have prevented the sun from rising."

﴿Then We made the sun over it an indication﴾, that is, We made the sun, by its removal of the shade when it comes, an indicator that the shade is a thing and a reality, because things are known by their opposites. Had there been no sun, the shade would not have been known, and had there been no light, darkness would not have been known. Thus al-dalil (the indicator) is on the pattern of fa'il in the sense of the active agent. It was also said: it is in the sense of the passive, like al-qatil (the slain), al-dahin (the oiled) and al-khadib (the dyed), meaning: We guided the sun to the shade until it took it away, that is, We made it follow the shade. So the sun is a dalil, that is, a proof and evidence, which reveals what is obscure and makes it clear. The word dalil was not made feminine even though it describes the sun, because it has the sense of a noun, as one says: "The sun is a proof" and "The sun is a truth."

﴿Then We withdrew it to Us, a gradual withdrawal﴾, meaning that shade which was extended.

﴿A gradual withdrawal to Us﴾, that is, its withdrawal is easy for Us, and everything in the command of our Lord is easy. The shade's stay in this atmosphere lasts from the break of dawn until sunrise. When the sun rises, the shade becomes withdrawn, and the sun's rays remain in this atmosphere in its place, shining upon the earth and upon things until the time of its setting. When it sets, there is no shade, and what remains is only the residual light of the day. Some people said: its withdrawal occurs at the sunset, because as long as the sun has not set, there remains some of the shade in it, and its disappearance is complete only with the coming of night and the entry of darkness upon it. It was also said: this withdrawal happens through the sun, because when it rises the shade begins to recede little by little. This was said by Abu Malik and Ibrahim al-Taymi. It was also said: "Then We withdrew it" means We withdrew the sun's light by means of the sun's rays, "a gradual withdrawal." It was also said: "gradual" means quick. This was said by al-Dahhak. Qatadah said: "gradual" means hidden, that is, when the sun sets, the shade is withdrawn in a hidden manner; whenever a part of it is withdrawn, a part of darkness is placed in its stead, and it does not vanish all at once. This is the meaning of Qatadah's statement, and it is also the view of Mujahid.

There are four issues in this verse.

The first concerns God's words: ﴿And He it is who made the night for you as a garment﴾, meaning a covering for creation that serves the purpose of clothing in concealing the body. Al-Tabari said: the night is described as a garment by way of comparison, in that it covers things and envelops them.

The second: Ibn al-'Arabi said: some heedless people thought that whoever prays naked in the darkness is valid in his prayer, because the night is a garment. This would mean that one may pray naked in one's house when one has closed one's door. Covering the body in prayer (al-sitr fi al-salah) is an act of worship in its own right and is not for the sake of people's gaze. There is no need to elaborate on this.

The third concerns God's words: ﴿and sleep as rest﴾, meaning a repose for your bodies through your cessation from occupations. The root of subat (sleep/rest) is stretching out. It is said: "the woman sabatat her hair," meaning she loosened it and let it down, and "a man who is masbut" meaning one of stretched-out build. It is said that sleep is called subat because it occurs through stretching out, and stretching out carries the sense of rest. It is also said: al-sabt means cutting off, so sleep is a cessation from occupation, and from this comes the Sabbath of the Jews, because they cease from work on it. It is also said: al-sabt means remaining in a place, so subat is a stillness and settling upon it, and sleep is a subat in the sense of being still and free from agitation and movement. Al-Khalil said: subat is heavy sleep, meaning: We made your sleep heavy so that refreshment and rest might be complete.

The fourth concerns God's words: ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾, from intishar (dispersal) for seeking livelihood; that is, the day is the cause of revival for dispersal. He likened wakefulness in it to the correspondence of revival with death. The Prophet (ﷺ), when he entered the morning, would say: "All praise is due to God who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection."

The Exalted said: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy﴾. This has been discussed fully in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 228. The reading "nashran" with the letter nun is the reading of Nafi'.]].

The Exalted said: ﴿And We send down from the sky pure water﴾. On this there are fifteen issues.

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿tahuran (pure water)﴾, meaning that by which one purifies, just as one says *wudu'* (ablution water) for the water with which one performs ablution. Every *tahur* (purifying) is *tahir* (pure), but not every *tahir* is *tahur*. *Al-tahur* (with a fatha on the ta') is the noun. The same applies to *al-wudu'* and *al-waqud*. With a damma it is the verbal noun, and this is the known usage in the lexicon, as stated by Ibn al-Anbari. So He made clear that the water sent down from the sky is pure in itself and purifying for others, since *tahur* is an intensive form of *tahir*, and this intensification requires that it be both pure and purifying. This is the view of the majority. It has also been said that *tahuran* means *tahir*, which is the view of Abu Hanifa, and he relied on His saying: ﴿And their Lord gave them to drink a pure drink﴾ [Al-Insan 76:21], meaning pure.

The poet says:

*O my two companions, is there in a glance, after repentance, a remedy by which I may heal my heart, though I am sinful?*
*Toward plump-buttocked, slender-waisted gazelles, sweet of teeth, whose saliva is pure.*

[[In Ibn al-'Arabi and Lisan al-'Arab, under the root *rjh*:
"Toward heavy-hipped ones, slender of waist."
A woman who is *rajjah* and *rajih* is one with heavy hindquarters, from a group of women with heavy hips.]]

He described the saliva as *tahur* (pure) and it is not purifying. The Arabs say: "a man who is *na'um* (a great sleeper)," and this does not mean that he causes others to sleep; rather it refers to his own action. Our scholars answered this and said: describing the drink of Paradise as *tahur* conveys purification from the filth of sins and from base qualities such as rancour and envy. When they drink this drink, God purifies them from the stain of sins and the filth of blameworthy beliefs, so they come to God with a sound heart and enter Paradise with the qualities of submission. It will be said to them then: ﴿Peace be upon you, you are good, so enter it, abiding forever﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:73]. Since its ruling in this world is the removal of the state of ritual impurity (*hadath*) by water flowing over the limbs, that was its wisdom in the Hereafter.

As for the poet's words "... *rikuhunna tahur*" (whose saliva is pure), he intended by this to exaggerate in describing the saliva as purifying, because of its sweetness, its attachment to hearts, its pleasantness in souls, and its quenching of the lover's thirst by sipping it, so that it is as if it were purifying water. In sum, the legal rulings are not established by poetic metaphor, for poets go beyond the bounds of truth into falsehood in their hyperbole, and they go on in speech until it leads them into innovation and disobedience, and sometimes they fall into disbelief without realizing it. Do you not see the saying of one of them:

*Had the surface of the earth not touched her foot, I would not have known the cause of tayammum (dry ablution).*

This is manifest disbelief; we seek refuge in God from it. The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: this is the furthest point of the essence of the scholars' speech, and it is comprehensive in its field. However, I have considered it from the standpoint of the Arabic language and found in it a bright dawn, namely that the pattern *fa'ul* is for intensification, yet intensification may occur in a transitive verb, as the poet said:

*A striker with the edge of the sword at the shins of their fat ones* [[This is the first half of a verse from an ode by Abu Talib ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib praising Musafir ibn 'Amr al-Qurashi, and its completion is:*
*When they lack provisions, you are a slaughterer.*]]

And it may occur in an intransitive verb, as the poet said:

*Sleeping late in the morning, she has not been girded for work* [[This is the second half of a verse from the mu'allaqa of Imru' al-Qays, and its first half is:*
*And in the morning she has wearied of musk on her bed.*
*Al-intiqat* means being girded for work. *Al-tafaddul* means wrapping oneself, which is wearing the least of one's garments.]]

The purifying quality of water for others is derived from what is beautiful in cleanliness, and from the Law in purity, as in His peace and blessings be upon him saying: "God does not accept a prayer without *tahur*" [[Narrated by Muslim.]]. The community has agreed, linguistically and legally, that the description *tahur* is specific to water and does not extend to the other liquids, even though they are pure. Their restricting it to water is therefore the strongest evidence that *tahur* means *mutahhir* (that which purifies). Another pattern, *fa'ul*, may come with another meaning, not from all this: it is an expression of the instrument of an act, not of the act itself, as in our saying *waqud* (fuel) and *sahur* (pre-dawn meal) with a fatha on the fa', for they are expressions of the firewood and the food eaten at pre-dawn. Thus describing water as *tahur* (with a fatha on the ta') is also a report about the instrument by which one purifies. When the fa' is given a damma in *waqud*, *sahur* and *tahur*, it returns to the act and is a report about the act. It is thereby established that the form *fa'ul* (with a fatha on the fa') may be an intensive form and may be a report about the instrument. This is what occurred to the Hanafis, but their jaws were too short to chew it [[An idiomatic expression meaning that they were unable to grasp it fully.]]. After this, clarification regarding the intensive and the instrumental rests on the evidence of His saying: ﴿And We send down from the sky pure water﴾. His peace and blessings be upon him also said: "The earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a *tahur*" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.]]. This may carry the intensive sense and may carry the sense of an instrument, so there is no proof in it for our scholars. But His saying "to purify you by it" [Al-Anfal 8:11] remains explicit that His action extends to others.

**The second issue:** Waters sent down from the sky and those stored in the earth are pure and purifying, despite the variation in their colours, tastes and odours, so long as nothing else mixes with them. What mixes with water is of three kinds:

The first kind agrees with water in both of its attributes. When it mixes with water and changes it, it does not deprive it of either attribute, because it agrees with both, and this is earth (*turab*).

The second kind agrees with water in one of its two attributes, which is purity. When it mixes with water and changes it, it deprives it of what it differs in, which is purifying, such as rose water and all other pure substances.

The third kind differs from water in both attributes. When it mixes with water and changes it, it deprives it of both attributes, because it differs from it in both, and this is impurity (*najis*).

**The third issue:** The Egyptian followers of Malik held that a small quantity of water is spoiled by a small amount of impurity, and that a large quantity is not spoiled unless it changes its colour, taste or smell by a forbidden substance. They did not set a boundary between the small and the large that one may stop at, except that Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik concerning a person in a major state of impurity who bathes in a pond of those ponds where animals are watered and who had not washed off the filth on him, that he had spoiled the water. This is the view of Ibn al-Qasim, Ashhab, Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and those who followed them among the Egyptians. Ibn Wahb alone says regarding water what the Medinan followers of Malik say. Their view, as Abu Mus'ab related from them and from him, is that water is not spoiled by impurity that enters it, whether little or much, unless the impurity appears in it and changes its taste, smell or colour. Ahmad ibn al-Mu'addal mentioned that this is the view of Malik ibn Anas regarding water. Ismail ibn Ishaq, Muhammad ibn Bukayr, Abu al-Faraj al-Abhari and all the adherents of Malik's school among the Baghdadis held this view, and it is the view of al-Awza'i, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Hasan ibn Salih and Dawud ibn 'Ali. It is also the view of the people of Basra, and it is the sound position in reasoning and in good transmitted reports.

Abu Hanifa said: if an impurity falls into water, it spoils it, whether much or little, when the impurity is certainly spread throughout it. The manner in which it is certain according to him is that a drop of urine falls into a pool. If the two edges of the pool move when one of them moves, the whole is impure; but if movement at one edge does not move the other, it does not become impure. The Majmu'a contains something similar to the view of Abu Hanifa.

Al-Shafi'i relied on the hadith of the two qullahs (*qullatayn*), and it is a disputed hadith, its chain and text having been questioned. Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and especially al-Daraqutni recorded it, for he began his book with it and gathered its routes. Ibn al-'Arabi said: al-Daraqutni, despite his standing as an imam, aimed to authenticate the hadith of the two qullahs but was unable to do so. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: as for what al-Shafi'i held regarding the hadith of the two qullahs, it is a weak position from the standpoint of reasoning and not established by transmission, because a group of the scholars of transmission have spoken against it, and because the actual measure of the two qullahs is not established by any sound report or consensus. If it were a binding limit, the scholars would have been obliged to investigate it in order to know the limit the Prophet ﷺ set, since it is part of the foundation of their religion and their obligation. Had it been so, they would not have neglected it, for they investigated matters less important and more subtle than this.

I say: what Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned of the disagreement concerning the two qullahs indicates that there is no divine determination (*tawqif*) on them nor a fixed measure. In the Sunan of al-Daraqutni, from Hammad ibn Zayd, from 'Asim ibn al-Mundhir, it is said: "the *qilal* are the large earthen jars." This 'Asim is one of the narrators of the hadith of the two qullahs. It appears from al-Daraqutni's words that they are like the *qilal* of Hajar, judging by his placing beside it the hadith of the Night Journey from Anas ibn Malik, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When I was raised to the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary in the seventh heaven, its fruit was like the *qilal* of Hajar and its leaves were like the ears of elephants," and he mentioned the hadith.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: our scholars relied on the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning the Well of Buda'a [[The Well of Buda'a: a well in Medina. It is said that Buda'a was the name of a woman to whom the well is attributed.]], which al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud and others transmitted. It is also a weak hadith with no standing in soundness, so no reliance is placed on it. I discussed this issue with al-Tusi al-Akbar, and he said: the most sincere of the positions on this matter is the position of Malik, for water is pure so long as none of its attributes has changed, since there is no hadith on the subject that may be relied upon. What is relied upon is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, which is His saying: ﴿And We send down from the sky pure water﴾ [Al-Furqan 25:48], and it is water with its attributes. So if it changes in any of them, it leaves the designation of water because it has left the attribute. For this reason, when al-Bukhari, the imam of hadith and jurisprudence, did not find a report on the subject that could be relied upon, he said: "Chapter: When the attribute of water changes," and he included the sound hadith: "No one is wounded in the cause of God—and God knows best who is wounded in His cause—but he will come on the Day of Resurrection with his wound flowing [[*Yaths'ab*: flowing.]] with blood, its colour the colour of blood and its smell the smell of musk." Thus the Prophet ﷺ informed that the blood remains as it is, and the fragrance of musk upon it does not remove it from the attribute of being blood.

For this reason our scholars said: if water changes by the smell of a carcass on its edge and shore, that does not prevent performing ablution with it. But if it changed by it while the carcass had been placed in it, that would make it impure through mixing. The first is contiguity, on which no reliance is placed.

I said: this has also been cited as evidence for the opposite ruling, namely that a change in its smell removes it from its original state. The reasoning is that when the blood's smell changed into the smell of musk, it ceased to be foul and impure, and became musk, and musk is part of the blood of the gazelle. Likewise, water whose smell has changed [is no longer in its original state]. The majority (al-Jumhur) adopted this interpretation regarding water, while 'Abd al-Malik adopted the first view. Abu 'Umar said: They made the ruling depend on the smell rather than the colour, so the ruling was attached to it, and they cited this hadith as evidence for it in their own opinion. But no meaning from it is understood that would satisfy the mind, nor is there in blood a meaning of water by which it could be compared. Jurists do not occupy themselves with such matters, and it is not the way of the people of knowledge to puzzle over it and make it obscure; rather their task is to clarify and explain it. For this reason, a covenant was taken from them that they would explain it to the people and not conceal it. Water's change is either caused by impurity or not caused by impurity. If it changed due to impurity, the scholars have agreed that it is neither pure nor purifying. Similarly, they agreed that if it changed without impurity, it remains pure in its original state. The majority said: it is not purifying, unless its change is from clay (turbah) and silt (hama'). What the scholars have agreed upon is the truth, which has no ambiguity and no confusion with it.

The fourth issue: water that has changed due to its bed, such as arsenic or a mineral that flows over it, or that has changed due to algae or tree leaves growing in it, which cannot be avoided. The scholars agreed that this does not prevent performing ablution with it, because it cannot be avoided and cannot be separated from it. Ibn Wahb, however, narrated from Malik that other water is preferable to it.

The fifth issue: Our scholars, may God have mercy upon them, said: the leftover water (su'r) of a Christian, of all unbelievers, of one who habitually drinks wine, and of one who eats carrion, such as dogs and others, is disliked. If someone performs ablution with their leftovers, there is nothing upon him unless he is certain of impurity. Al-Bukhari said: 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) performed ablution from the house of a Christian woman. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna mentioned, saying: "Narrate to us from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, who said: When we were in al-Sham, I brought Umar ibn al-Khattab water and he performed ablution with it. He said: Where did you get this water? I have never seen water sweeter, nor rainwater more pure than it. I said: I brought it from the house of this Christian old woman. When he had performed ablution, he went to her and said: O old woman, embrace Islam and you will be safe; God sent Muhammad (ﷺ) with the truth. She uncovered her head, and it was like the thaghama [[al-Thaghama: a plant with white fruit and flowers, resembling white hair.]], and she said: I am an old woman, and I am about to die now! 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) said: O God, bear witness." Al-Daraqutni narrated it: al-Husayn ibn Isma'il told us, that Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Bushanji told us, that Sufyan told us... and he mentioned it. He also narrated it from al-Husayn ibn Isma'il, who said: Khallad ibn Aslam told us, Sufyan told us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) performed ablution from the house of a Christian woman; he went to her and said: O old woman, embrace Islam... and he mentioned the hadith similar to what preceded.

The sixth issue: As for a dog that laps up water, Malik said: the vessel is washed seven times and one does not perform ablution with it, though the water remains pure. Al-Thawri said: one performs ablution with that water and makes tayammum along with it. This is also the view of 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and Muhammad ibn Maslama. Abu Hanifa said: the dog is impure, so the vessel is washed from it because it is impure. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq. Malik used to distinguish, regarding washing the vessel after a dog has lapped from it, between dogs whose keeping is permitted and dogs whose keeping is not permitted. The summary of his position is that it is pure in his view, and its lapping does not make impure anything it laps into, whether food or other things; however, he recommended pouring out the water it has lapped, for the sake of the small cost. The dog of the desert and the dog of the town are the same. The vessel is washed from it in every case seven times as an act of worship (ta'abbud). This is what his position settled upon among his debating students. Ibn Wahb mentioned, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam told us, from his father, from 'Ata', from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the pools between Makka and Madina, and it was said to him: Dogs and beasts of prey come to them. He said: "No. What they have taken into their bellies is theirs, and what remains is for us, a drink and a purifier." Al-Daraqutni narrated it. This is an explicit text on the purity of dogs and the purity of what they lap from. In al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Umar, it is reported that dogs used to come and go in the mosque of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they did not sprinkle any of that. 'Umar said in the presence of the Companions, to the owner of the pool whom 'Amr ibn al-'As asked: Do beasts of prey come to your pool? 'Umar said: O owner of the pool, do not inform us, for we come to beasts of prey and they come to us. Malik and al-Daraqutni narrated it. He did not distinguish among beasts of prey, and the dog is among them. There is no proof for the opponent in the command to pour out what it has lapped, nor that this is due to impurity. He commanded that it be poured out only because the soul abhors it, not because of impurity, since keeping oneself free from filth is recommended. Or it is a severity upon them, because they were forbidden from keeping them, as Ibn 'Umar and al-Hasan said; so when they did not desist, severity was imposed upon them regarding water, given its scarcity among them in the desert, so that it would be hard on them and they would refrain from keeping them. As for the command to wash the vessel, it is an act of worship and not because of impurity, as we have mentioned, for two reasons. The first: washing has been attached to a number. The second: earth has been given a role in it, by his statement (peace be upon him): "And rub it with earth as the eighth [washing]." Had it been due to impurity, there would be neither a number nor a role for earth in it, as with urine. The Prophet (peace be upon him) also declared the cat and what it laps from to be pure, and the cat is a beast of prey, without any disagreement on that, since it hunts and eats carrion. Likewise the dog and what is similar to it among the beasts of prey, for when a text concerning one of them comes, it is a text concerning the other. This is among the strongest kinds of analogy (qiyas). This is so even if there were no other evidence, and we have mentioned the explicit text on its purity, so the opponent's view falls. And praise be to God.

The seventh issue: Whatever dies in water and has no blood does not harm the water, provided it does not change its smell; if it becomes foul-smelling, one may not perform ablution with it. Likewise, what has flowing blood among aquatic animals, such as fish and frogs, its death in the water does not corrupt that water, unless its smell changes. If its smell changes and it becomes foul, it is not permissible to purify oneself with it or perform ablution from it. According to Malik it is not impure. As for what has flowing blood and dies in water, if it is removed from the place and its colour, taste and smell have not changed, it is pure and purifying, whether the water is little or much, according to the people of Madina. Some of them recommended removing buckets of that water so that the soul may be at ease with it, and they do not set a limit that may not be exceeded. They dislike using that water before the buckets are removed; if someone uses it for bathing or ablution, it is permissible, provided its condition is as we have described. Some of Malik's companions held that whoever performs ablution with this water, even if it has not changed, should perform tayammum as well, combining the two purifications as a precaution; if he does not do so and prays with that water, it suffices him. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Muhammad ibn Sirin that a black man fell into Zamzam, that is, and died; Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him) ordered him to be taken out, and ordered the water to be drawn out. He said: A spring came to them from the corner, overwhelming them, so he ordered that it be stopped with cloth from Qibt and with striped silks, until they drew it out; when they had drawn it out, it gushed forth over them. He also narrated from Abu al-Tufayl that a boy fell into the well of Zamzam and it was drawn out. This may indicate that the water had changed, and God knows best. Shu'ba narrated from Mughira from Ibrahim that he used to say: Every creature with flowing blood, ablution is not performed from it; but leniency was granted regarding the beetle, the scorpion, the locust and the jadjad [[al-Jadjad: a small bird resembling a locust.]] when they fall into the water-skin [[al-Rika' (pl. of rakwa): a small leather vessel from which water is drunk.]], so there is no harm in it. Shu'ba said: I think he mentioned the gecko as well. Al-Daraqutni narrated it: al-Husayn ibn Isma'il told us, Muhammad ibn al-Walid told us, Muhammad ibn Ja'far told us, Shu'ba told us... and he mentioned it.

The eighth issue: The majority of the Companions, the jurists of the cities, and all the Successors in Hijaz and Iraq, held that what the cat has lapped from water is pure, and there is no harm in performing ablution with its leftovers, based on the hadith of Abu Qatada, which Malik and others narrated. There is disagreement on this from Abu Hurayra. It is narrated from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Muhammad ibn Sirin that they ordered the pouring out of water that a cat had lapped from, and the washing of the vessel from it. There is disagreement on this from al-Hasan. It is possible that al-Hasan saw impurity in its mouth, so that the two narrations from him can be reconciled. al-Tirmidhi, when he mentioned the hadith of Malik, said: "On this subject, there are also reports from 'A'isha and Abu Hurayra. This hadith is good and sound, and it is the view of most people of knowledge among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), the Successors and those after them, such as al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq, who saw no harm in the leftovers of a cat. This is the best thing on this subject, and Malik perfected this hadith from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Talha, and no one has narrated it more completely than Malik." The hafiz Abu 'Umar said: The proof in case of dispute and disagreement is the Sunna of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and it is authentically established from the hadith of Abu Qatada that he tilted the vessel for her until she drank. The hadith... Upon it rely the jurists in every city except Abu Hanifa and those who follow his view, for he disliked her leftovers. He said: If someone performs ablution with it, it suffices. I know of no better argument for those who disliked performing ablution with the cat's leftovers than that the hadith of Abu Qatada did not reach him, while the hadith of Abu Hurayra about the dog did reach him, so he analogized the cat to the dog. And it has been distinguished

The Sunnah between them is on the matter of acts of worship (ta'abbud) in washing a vessel. Whoever is argued for by the Sunnah has been defeated in dispute, and whatever contradicts it is rejected. Success is from God.

Among their arguments also is what Qurrah ibn Khalid narrated from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The purification of a vessel into which a cat has lapped is that it be washed once or twice." Qurrah was in doubt. This hadith was not traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ) except by Qurrah ibn Khalid, and Qurrah is trustworthy and firm (thiqah thabt).

I say: this hadith was transmitted by al-Daraqutni, and its text is: "The purification of a vessel into which a dog has lapped is that it be washed seven times, the first with earth, and [for] the cat, once or twice." Qurrah was in doubt.

Abu Bakr said: Abu 'Asim narrated it in this way, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report, while others narrated from Qurrah the lapping of the dog as marfu' and the lapping of the cat as mawquf (ending with Abu Hurayrah). Abu Salih narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A vessel is washed from the cat as it is washed from the dog." Al-Daraqutni said: This is not established as marfu'; what is preserved is the saying of Abu Hurayrah, and it has been differently reported from him. Ma'mar and Ibn Jurayj mentioned, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, that he used to treat the cat like the dog. And from Mujahid that he said, concerning a vessel into which a cat (sinnawr) has lapped: "Wash it seven times." Al-Daraqutni said.

The ninth point: Water that has been used is pure, provided the limbs of the one performing ablution with it were pure. However, Malik and a group of the eminent jurists disliked performing ablution with it. Malik said: "There is no good in it, and I do not like anyone to perform ablution with it. If someone does so and prays, I do not see that he must repeat the prayer, but he should perform ablution for what follows." Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i and their companions said: It is not permissible to use it to remove ritual impurity (raf' al-hadath), and whoever performs ablution with it must repeat (the prayer), because it is not unrestricted water (ma' mutlaq), and whoever finds it should perform tayammum, because he is not one who finds water. Asbagh ibn al-Faraj agreed with their view in this, and it is the view of al-Awza'i.

They relied on the hadith of al-Sunabihi, which Malik transmitted, and the hadith of 'Amr ibn 'Anbasah, which Muslim transmitted, and other reports. They also said: When water is used for ablution, the sins come out with it, so it is necessary to keep away from it, because it is water of sins. Abu 'Umar said: This, in my view, has no basis, because sins do not render water impure, since they have no bodies or substances that mix with water and corrupt it. The meaning of his saying "the sins came out with the water" is only a declaration from him that ablution for prayer is an act by which God expiates evil deeds for His believing servants, out of His mercy toward them and His bounty upon them.

Abu Thawr and Dawud said, like the view of Malik, that performing ablution with used water is permissible, because it is pure water that has not been mixed with anything, and it is unrestricted water. They relied on the consensus of the community (ijma' al-ummah) that it is pure when there is no impurity on the limbs of the one performing ablution. This was also the view of Abu 'Abd Allah al-Marwazi, Muhammad ibn Nasr.

It is also reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Umamah, 'Ata ibn Abi Rabah, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Nakha'i, Makhul and al-Zuhri that they said, concerning one who forgot to wipe his head and found moisture in his beard, that it suffices for him to wipe his head with that moisture. All of these permitted performing ablution with used water.

'Abd al-Salam ibn Salih narrated to us: Ishaq ibn Suwayd narrated to us, from al-'Ala' ibn Ziyad, from a man of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who was trustworthy (marḍi): that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out to them one day after he had bathed, and a patch of his body remained which the water had not reached. We said: "O Messenger of God, this is a patch which the water did not reach." He had long hair (sha'r warid) [[i.e., flowing and long.]], so he said [[The Arabs use the word "qala" (said) as an expression for all actions, and apply it to other than speech and tongue. So they say: qala bi-yadihi, meaning he took; qala bi-rijlihi, meaning he walked; qala bi-l-ma'i 'ala yadihi, meaning he turned; qala bi-thawbin, meaning he raised it. All of this is by way of metaphor and extension.]] by his hair, thus, upon the place, and wetted it. Al-Daraqutni narrated it and said: 'Abd al-Salam ibn Salih is a Basran and not strong, while others among the trustworthy narrators report it from Ishaq, from al-'Ala' as a mursal (report lacking a Companion), and this is the correct one.

I say: The trustworthy narrator from Ishaq ibn Suwayd al-'Adawi, from al-'Ala' ibn Ziyad al-'Adawi, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) bathed... the hadith, as recorded by Hushaym.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The matter of used water is built upon another principle, which is whether an instrument with which an obligatory act has been fulfilled may be used to fulfil another obligatory act. The opponent prohibited this by analogy with the slave: when a slave has been freed to fulfil an obligation of manumission, he cannot be used again to fulfil another obligation. This is a false statement, for when manumission takes effect on the state of slavery it destroys it, so no place remains for fulfilling an obligation by another manumission. Its counterpart in water is what is lost on the limbs, for it cannot be validly used for another obligation because its substance has been sensibly lost, just as slavery is lost in the slave by manumission as a legal effect. This is precious, so reflect upon it."

**The tenth issue:** Malik and his companions did not distinguish between water into which an impurity falls and an impurity onto which water flows, whether the water is still or flowing. Their evidence is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Water is not made impure by anything, except what overpowers it and changes its taste, colour, or smell." The Shafi'is made a distinction. They said: when an impurity falls onto water, the water becomes impure. Ibn al-'Arabi chose this view and said: "Among the principles of the Shari'ah concerning the rulings on water is that an impurity falling onto water is not like water flowing onto an impurity, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'When one of you wakes from his sleep, he should not dip his hand into the vessel until he has washed it three times, for none of you knows where his hand spent the night.' He forbade the hand from entering the water and commanded that water be poured over it. This is a wonderful principle in this matter. Had the water not been poured onto the impurity, whether little or much, it would not have been purified." It is also established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said, regarding the urine of the Bedouin in the mosque: "Pour a *dhanub* [[The *dhanub* (with a fatha): a bucket.]] of water over it." Our shaykh Abu al-'Abbas said: They also used as evidence the hadith of the two qullahs. They said: if the water is less than two qullahs and an impurity falls into it, it becomes impure even if it does not change it. But if that amount of water flows onto the impurity and removes its substance, the water remains pure and has removed the impurity. This is a contradiction, since mixing has occurred in both cases. Their distinction between water flowing onto an impurity and an impurity falling onto water is a formal distinction with no understanding of jurisprudence in it. This matter is not one of acts of worship (ta'abbudat) but one of rational meanings, for it concerns the removal of impurity and its rulings. Moreover, all of this is refuted by his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him: "Water is pure and purifying; nothing makes it impure, except what changes its colour, taste, or smell." I say: This hadith was narrated by al-Daraqutni from Rishdin ibn Sa'd Abu al-Hajjaj, from Mu'awiya ibn Salih, from Rashid ibn Sa'd, from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, and from Thawban, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it contains no mention of colour. He said: No one raised it except Rishdin ibn Sa'd from Mu'awiya ibn Salih, and he is not strong. A better hadith for argument is what Abu Usamah narrated from al-Walid ibn Kathir, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, from 'Ubaydullah ibn 'Abdullah ibn Rafi' ibn Khadij, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: It was said, "O Messenger of Allah, shall we perform ablution from the well of Bud'ah?" It is a well into which menstrual rags [[The *hiyad* (menstrual rags): the cloths used to wipe menstrual blood; they are also called *mahayid*.]], the flesh of dogs, and filth are thrown. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, water is pure; nothing makes it impure." Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Daraqutni all narrated it with this chain. Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a good hadith, and Abu Usamah has excelled in narrating it; no one has narrated the hadith of Abu Sa'id concerning the well of Bud'ah better than Abu Usamah." This hadith is explicit about an impurity falling onto water, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ruled that it remains pure and purifying. Abu Dawud said: I heard Qutaybah ibn Sa'id say: "I asked the custodian of the well of Bud'ah about its depth. I asked, 'What is the most water it contains?' He said, 'Up to the waist.' I asked, 'And when it decreases?' He said, 'Below the navel.'" Abu Dawud said: "I measured the well of Bud'ah with my cloak, stretching it over the well, then I measured it with a cubit, and its width was six cubits. I asked the one who opened the garden gate for me and let me enter: 'Has its structure been changed from what it was?' He said, 'No.' I saw water in it that was discoloured." This was evidence for us of what we have mentioned, except that Ibn al-'Arabi said: "It was in the middle of a salt marsh, so its water would be discoloured by its bed, and Allah knows best." **The eleventh issue:** The pure, purifying water with which ablution (wudu') and washing impurities are permitted is clear water from the sky, rivers, seas, springs, and wells, and whatever people know as water without qualification, not combined with anything that mixes with it, as Allah, mighty and majestic, created it, clear. The colour of its ground does not harm it, as we have explained. Abu Hanifa, 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar disagreed on this general matter. As for Abu Hanifa, he permitted ablution with nabidh (a drink made by steeping dates or raisins in water) while travelling, and he allowed removing impurity with any pure liquid. As for oil and broth, there is a report from him that it is not permissible to remove impurity with them. However, his companions say: if the impurity is removed with them, it is permissible. Likewise with fire and the sun. Indeed, the hide of a carcass that dries in the sun becomes pure without tanning. Likewise, an impurity on the ground that dries in the sun, the place becomes pure, so that prayer may be performed on it, but tayammum (dry ablution with earth) may not be performed with that dust. Ibn al-'Arabi said: When Allah, glorified is He, described water as *tahur* (purifying) and bestowed favour in sending it down from the sky to purify us with it, this indicates that it is specific to that. Likewise, the Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said to Asma' daughter of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq when she asked him about menstrual blood that gets on a garment: "Rub it, then scrape it, then wash it with water." Therefore, other than water is not equated with water, because doing so would nullify the favour. Impurity is not a perceptible substance so that it could be said that whatever removes it has fulfilled the purpose. Rather, impurity is a legal ruling for which the Lawgiver specified water, so nothing else is equated with it, since it is not in its meaning. Moreover, if it were equated with it, it would cancel it, and when a branch's being equated with its root results in its cancelling it, the branch itself is cancelled. Tāj al-Sunnah dhu al-'Izz Ibn al-Murtada al-Dabusi used to call this "the offspring of fornication." I say: As for what has been used as evidence for the use of nabidh, the hadiths are weak and frail, none of which stands on its own legs. al-Daraqutni mentioned them, declared them weak, and stated this explicitly. Likewise, what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas as a statement of his own, "Nabidh is ablution for one who does not find water," has been declared weak, because its chain includes Ibn Muhriz, who is abandoned in hadith. Likewise, what is narrated from 'Ali, that he said: "There is no harm in performing ablution with nabidh," has al-Hajjaj and Abu Layla, who are both weak. The hadith of Ibn Mas'ud has been declared weak, and it was said: "Only Ibn Lahi'a narrated it, and he is weak in hadith." It is also mentioned from 'Alqamah ibn Qays that he said: "I said to 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: 'Did any of you witness the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night the jinn's summoner came to him?' He said, 'No.'" I say: This chain is authentic, and there is no disagreement about the reliability of its narrators. al-Tirmidhi also narrated the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) asked me: 'What is in your *idawa* [[The *idawa* (with a kasra): a small vessel made of leather for water.]]?' I said, 'Nabidh.' He said: 'A good date and pure water.'" He said: "So he performed ablution with it." Abu 'Isa said: "This hadith is narrated only from Abu Zayd, from 'Abdullah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Abu Zayd is an unknown man according to the people of hadith; we do not know any narration from him other than this hadith. Some scholars held the view that ablution with nabidh is valid, among them Sufyan and others. Some scholars said: One does not perform ablution with nabidh, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq. Ishaq said: 'If a man is afflicted with this, and he performs ablution with nabidh and then tayammum, it is more beloved to me.'" Abu 'Isa said: "The view of those who say that one does not perform ablution with nabidh is closer to the Book and the Sunnah and more consistent with them, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then you do not find water, so perform tayammum with clean earth﴾." This issue is extensively discussed in books of disagreement (al-khilaf), and their main reliance is on the wording "water," as was explained earlier in *al-Ma'idah* [[See vol. 6, p. 105 and following, first or second edition.]]. Allah knows best. **The twelfth issue:** When Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water, purifying﴾, and said: ﴿to purify you thereby﴾, a group hesitated regarding seawater, because it was not sent down from the sky. They even narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Amr together that one should not perform ablution with it, because it is fire and because it is the lid of Hell. But the Prophet (ﷺ) clarified its ruling when he said to one who asked him: "Its water is purifying, and its dead animals are lawful," narrated by Malik. Abu 'Isa said of it: "This is a good, authentic hadith." It is the view of most jurists among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), including Abu Bakr, 'Umar, and Ibn 'Abbas, who saw no harm in seawater. Some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) disliked performing ablution with seawater, including Ibn 'Umar and 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr said: "It is fire." Abu 'Umar said: Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi was asked about this hadith of Malik, narrated from Safwan ibn Sulaym, and he said: "In my view it is an authentic hadith." Abu 'Isa said: I said to al-Bukhari: "Hushaym says that Ibn Abi Barzah is mentioned in it." He said: "He erred in it; it is al-Mughira ibn Abi Burdah." Abu 'Umar said: I do not know what this is from al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him. Had it been authentic, he would have included it in his authentic compilation, and he did not, because he relies in the authentic (*sahih*) only on the chain. The people of hadith do not rely on a chain like this one, yet in my view it is authentic, because the scholars received it with acceptance and acted upon it, and none of the jurists disagrees with its overall content; the disagreement among them concerns only some of its meanings. A majority of scholars and a group of leading jurists in the regions have agreed that the sea is pure in its water and that ablution with it is permissible, except what was narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, that they both disliked performing ablution with seawater. No other jurist of the regions followed them in this, nor did anyone give it weight or pay attention to it, given the hadith on this subject. This indicates to you that the hadith is well known among them, that they act upon it and accept it, and it is preferable to them over an apparently sound chain when its meaning is rejected by the fundamental principles. And success is from Allah.

Abu 'Umar said: Safwan ibn Sulaym, the mawla of Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf al-Zuhri, was one of the worshippers of the people of Madina and the most God-fearing of them, an ascetic, abundant in charity with whatever he found, great and small, abundant in good deeds, fearful of God. His kunya was Abu 'Abd Allah. He settled in Madina and did not move away from it, and he died there in the year 132 AH. 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal reported: I heard my father being asked about Safwan ibn Sulaym, and he said: "Reliable (thiqa), one of the best of God's servants and the most excellent of the Muslims."

As for Sa'id ibn Salama, to the best of my knowledge no one narrated from him except Safwan, and God knows best. Whoever is in this condition is unknown (majhul), and no proof is established by him according to all of them.

As for al-Mughira ibn Abi Burda, it was said of him that he is not well known among the bearers of knowledge, like Sa'id ibn Salama. It was also said: he is not unknown. Abu 'Umar said: I found mention of al-Mughira ibn Abi Burda in the campaigns (maghazi) of Musa ibn Nusayr in the Maghrib, and Musa employed him over the cavalry, and God granted him conquests in the lands of the Berbers, by land and by sea.

al-Daraqutni narrated, through a route other than Malik, from Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is not purified by the water of the sea, may God not purify him." He said: its isnad is hasan.

The thirteenth: Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some people imagined that if a person in a state of major impurity (junub) leaves a surplus of water, it may not be used for ablution; this is a false doctrine. It is established from Maymuna that she said: "I and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were both in a state of major impurity, and I bathed from a large vessel (jafna) and some water was left over. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to bathe from it, and I said: 'I have already bathed from it.' He said: 'Indeed water is not made impure (laysa 'alayhi najasa)' — or: 'water does not become junub.'"

Abu 'Umar said: Reports have come on this subject, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), prohibiting a man from performing ablution with the leftover water of a woman. Some of them add: "But let both of you scoop together." One group said: it is not permissible for a man to scoop together with a woman from one vessel, because each of them would be performing ablution with the leftover of the other. Others said: what is disliked is only that a woman should be alone with the vessel and then a man performs ablution with her leftover after her. Each of them narrated reports supporting what they held. What the majority of scholars and the jurists of the major cities hold is that there is no harm in a man performing ablution with a woman's leftover, and a woman performing ablution with a man's leftover, whether the woman was alone with the vessel or not. There are many sound reports on this matter. What we hold is that water is not made impure by anything except those impurities that appear in it or predominate over it; there is no point in occupying oneself with reports and statements that are not authentic. And God is the One sought for help.

al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Maymuna told me: "I and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to bathe from one vessel in a state of major impurity (janaba)." He said: this is a hadith hasan sahih.

al-Bukhari narrated from 'A'isha, who said: "I and the Prophet (ﷺ) used to bathe from one vessel called the faraq [[al-faraq (with a vowel on the ra): a measure holding sixteen ratl. With a sukun: a measure of one hundred and twenty ratl.]]."

In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to bathe with the leftover of Maymuna.

al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: One of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) bathed in a jafna, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wanted to perform ablution from it.
