She said: "O Messenger of God, I was in a state of major impurity." He said: "Indeed water does not become junub." He said: this is a hadith hasan sahih, and it is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri, Malik and al-Shafi'i.

al-Daraqutni narrated from 'Amra, from 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, who said: "I and the Prophet (ﷺ) used to perform ablution from one vessel, and a cat had drunk from it before that." He said: this is a hadith hasan sahih.

It is also related from a man of the Banu Ghifar who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade the leftover purifying water of a woman. And on this subject there is a report from 'Abd Allah ibn Sarjis. Some jurists disliked the leftover purifying water of a woman, and this is the view of Ahmad and Ishaq.

The fourteenth: al-Daraqutni narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, mawla of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab had water heated for him in a qumqumma [[al-qumqumma and al-qumqum (like hudhud): a vessel of copper or other material in which water is heated.]] and he bathed with it. He said: this isnad is sahih.

It is related from 'A'isha, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) entered when I had heated water in the sun, and he said: "Do not do this, O Humayra, for it causes leucoderma (baras)." This was transmitted by Khalid ibn Isma'il al-Makhzumi from Hisham ibn 'Urwa from his father from 'A'isha, and he is matruk (abandoned). It was also transmitted by 'Amr ibn Muhammad al-A'sham from Fulayh from al-Zuhri from 'Urwa from 'A'isha, and he is munkar al-hadith; no one other than him narrated it from Fulayh, and it is not authentic from al-Zuhri, as said by al-Daraqutni.

The fifteenth: Every pure vessel is permissible for performing ablution from, except vessels of gold and silver, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition of using them. And that, God knows best, is for the sake of resembling foreigners and tyrants, not because of any impurity in them. Whoever performs ablution from them, his ablution suffices him, but he is sinful for using them. It has been said: ablution is not valid from either of them. The first view is the more common, as Abu 'Umar said. Every tanned hide that has been slaughtered (dhaki) is permissible to use for ablution and other purposes. Malik used to dislike performing ablution from a vessel made of the hide of a dead animal after tanning, with a difference in his opinion. This has been discussed in "al-Nahl" [[See vol. 10, p. 156, first or second edition.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 49:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That We may give life thereby﴾, i.e., by the rain.

(a dead land) barren through drought, lifeless and without vegetation. Ka'b said: "Rain is the spirit of the earth; Allah gives it life through it." He said "maytan" (dead, masculine) and did not say "maytatan" (feminine) because the meaning of "al-baldah" (land) and "al-balad" (land/town) is one; so said al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, a grammarian). It has also been said: he intended by "al-balad" the place.

(and give it to drink) is the reading of the common readers, with a ḍammah on the nūn (nusqiya, "nusqiyahu"). But ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, ʿAsim, and al-Aʿmash, as transmitted by al-Mufaddal from them, read "nasqiyahu" with a fatḥah on the nūn. [[In the manuscripts: "with a ḍammah on the nūn." This is an error; the correction is from Abu Hayyan and others.]]

(of what We have created, cattle and many people). I.e., many human beings. Anasiyy is the singular of insiyy, like the plural of qurqur (a kind of ship): qarāqīr and qarāqir, according to al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, and one of two opinions of al-Farra'. He also has another view: its singular is insān, then the nūn is changed to a yā', so one says anāsī, the original being anāsīn, like sirḥān and sarāḥīn, and bustān and basātīn; they made the yā' a substitute for the nūn. On this basis, sarāḥī and basātī are also permissible, with no difference between them. Al-Farra' said: anāsī is also permissible with the yā' between the lām and the ʿayn of the root lightened, like qarāqīr and qarāqir. He said "kathīran" (many) and did not say "kathīrīn," because fa'īl may be intended to denote abundance, as in "wa-ḥasuna ulā'ika rafīqan" (and excellent are those as companions). [[See vol. 5, p. 271 and following.]]

Allah's statement: ﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them﴾, meaning the Qur'an, and its mention has already occurred at the beginning of the surah, where Allah says: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan)﴾. And (the verse) "Indeed, he led me away from the reminder after it had come to me" and His statement: "Indeed, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned."

(﴿That they may take heed, but most of the people refused except in ingratitude﴾), i.e., denial of it and rejection of it. It has also been said that "And We have certainly distributed it among them" refers to the rain. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud: there is no year with more rain than another, but Allah distributes it wherever He wills, so that what is increased for some is decreased for others. This is the meaning of tasrif (distribution). It has also been said: "We distributed it among them" as heavy rain, downpour, light rain, drizzle (rihам) and fine mist (raddhad). Al-Jawhari said: ar-rihам are gentle rains. It has also been said: its distribution is the variation of benefit derived from it in drinking, watering, agriculture, purification, irrigating gardens, bathing and the like.

﴿That they may take heed, but most of the people refused except in ingratitude﴾. 'Ikrimah said: this refers to their saying about the stars (anwa'): "We were given rain by the star of such-and-such." An-Nahhas said: we know of no disagreement among the people of tafsir that the kufr here is their saying "We were given rain by such-and-such a star," and that its like is "the star did such-and-such," and that whoever attributes an action to it is a disbeliever. Ar-Rabi' ibn Subayh narrated: the people were given rain during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one night, and when morning came the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "In the morning people are of two kinds: a grateful one and a disbelieving one. As for the grateful one, he praises Allah for His watering and His relief; as for the disbeliever, he says: We were given rain by such-and-such a star."

It is also narrated from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no year with more rain than another, but when a people engage in sins, Allah turns that (rain) away to others; and when they all disobey, Allah turns it away to the wastelands and the seas."

It has also been said that the tasrif refers to the wind, and its explanation has already passed in al-Baqarah. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "liyadhkuru" with a light dhal from dhikr (remembrance). The rest read it with a doubled dhal from tadhakkur (taking heed), meaning: that they may remember the blessings of Allah and know that the one who bestows them must not be associated with partners. So tadhakkur is close to dhikr, except that tadhakkur is used for what has gone far from the heart, so it requires effort in remembering.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised up in every town a warner﴾, meaning a messenger to warn them, just as We distributed the rain. This was so that the burdens of prophethood would be lighter upon you. But We did not do that; rather, We made you a warner for all, so that your rank would be elevated. So be thankful for the favour of Allah upon you.

(So do not obey the disbelievers) meaning, in what they call you to of following their gods.

(And strive against them with it) Ibn 'Abbas said: with the Qur'an. Ibn Zayd said: with Islam. It was also said: with the sword, but this is far-fetched, because the surah is Meccan and was revealed before the command to fight.

(A great striving) without any slackening accompanying it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised up in every town a warner﴾, meaning a messenger to warn them, just as We distributed the rain. This was so that the burdens of prophethood would be lighter upon you. But We did not do that; rather, We made you a warner for all, so that your rank would be elevated. So be thankful for the favour of Allah upon you.

(So do not obey the disbelievers) meaning, in what they call you to of following their gods.

(And strive against them with it) Ibn 'Abbas said: with the Qur'an. Ibn Zayd said: with Islam. It was also said: with the sword, but this is far-fetched, because the surah is Meccan and was revealed before the command to fight.

(A great striving) without any slackening accompanying it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is He who released the two seas﴾. The discourse has returned to the mention of blessings. *Maraja* (مَرَجَ) means to let loose, to mix, and to send forth. Mujahid said: He sent them forth and poured one of them into the other. Ibn 'Arafa said: "Maraja al-bahrayn" means He mixed them, so that they meet. It is said: "I *marajtuhu*" when I mixed it. *Maraja* also applies to a matter or a religion when it becomes confused and disordered, and from this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in a confused matter﴾ (fi amrin marij). From the same root is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As [[The hadith concerns tribulation (fitnah).]]: "When you see the people's covenants become confused (*maragat*) and their trusts diminished, and they become like this and like this," and he interlaced his fingers. I said to him: "What should I do in that case, may God make me your ransom!" He said: "Keep to your house, hold your tongue, take what you recognise, leave what you reject, and attend to the particular matter of yourself, and leave aside the affair of the common people." It was related by al-Nasa'i, Abu Dawud and others. Al-Azhari said: "Maraja al-bahrayn" means he left them free between them; it is said "*marajtu al-dabbata*" when I let the animal graze freely. Tha'lab said: *al-marj* is making to run, so His saying "maraja al-bahrayn" means He made them run. Al-Akhfash said: some people say *amraja al-bahrayn*, like *maraja*; *fa'ala* and *af'ala* have the same meaning.

﴿This is sweet, palatable (*furat*)﴾: that is, sweet, extremely fresh.

﴿And this is salty, bitter (*ujaj*)﴾: that is, it has saltiness and bitterness. It is reported from Talha that he read "wa hadha milhun" with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam.

﴿And He placed between them a barrier (*barzakh*)﴾: that is, a partition from His power, so that neither of them overcomes the other, as He said in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿He released the two seas, meeting together. Between them is a barrier which they do not transgress﴾.

﴿And a forbidding ban (*hijran mahjuran*)﴾: that is, a concealed veil that prevents one of them from mixing with the other. So *al-barzakh* is the barrier, and *al-hijr* is the preventer. Al-Hasan said: it means the Sea of Persia and the Sea of Rome. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: it means the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth. Ibn 'Abbas said: they meet every year, and between them is a barrier, a decree from His decrees. ﴿A forbidding ban (*hijran mahjuran*)﴾: forbidden and prohibited, that this salt should become sweet through the sweet, or that this sweet should become salty through the salt.

**Second issue in this verse: the words of Allah, the Exalted:** ﴿And it is He who created from water a human being﴾, meaning He created a human from a drop of semen.

**﴿So He made him a relative by lineage and by marriage﴾**, meaning He made the human being a *nasab* (blood lineage) and a *sihr* (marital kinship).

It was also said that "from water" points to the origin of creation, since every living thing is created from water. This verse counts among the blessings Allah bestowed on people by bringing them into existence after they were not, and it calls attention to the lesson in that.

**The second issue:** Allah's words: ﴿So He made him a relative by lineage and by marriage﴾. *Nasab* and *sihr* are two meanings that cover every kinship that exists between two human beings.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: *Nasab* refers to the mixing of water between the male and the female in the manner prescribed by the Shari'ah. If it occurs through sin, it is mere physical creation and not an established lineage. For this reason, his daughter from fornication does not fall under Allah's words, "Prohibited to you are your mothers and your daughters" (4:23), because she is not truly his daughter according to the more correct of the two opinions of our scholars and the more correct of the two opinions in the religion. If no lineage exists in the Shari'ah, then no *sihr* exists in the Shari'ah either. Therefore, fornication does not make a man's daughter's daughter, or a woman's daughter's mother, forbidden. What is forbidden from lawful relations is not forbidden from unlawful ones, because Allah bestowed favor upon His servants through *nasab* and *sihr*, elevated their status, and attached the rulings on permissibility and prohibition to them. Therefore falsehood does not attach to them, nor does it equal them.

I say: The jurists have differed concerning a man marrying his daughter from fornication, or his sister, or his son's daughter from fornication. Some prohibited this, among them Ibn al-Qasim, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. Others permitted it, among them Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. This matter has already been discussed fully in *al-Nisa'* [[See vol. 5, p. 114 and following, first or second edition.]].

Al-Farra' said: *Nasab* is the lineage whose marriage is not permitted. Al-Zajjaj also said this, and it is the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

The derivation of *sihr* is from *sahartu al-shay'* when I mixed the thing. Each of the two in-law parties has mixed with the other, so marriages were called *sihr* because people mix with one another through them. It was also said: *sihr* is the kinship of marriage. The wife's relatives are the *akhtan*, and the husband's relatives are the *ahma'*. The term *asman* applies generally to all of them. This was said by al-Asma'i.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: The *akhtan* are the wife's father and her brother and her paternal uncle, as al-Asma'i said. The *sihr* is the husband of a man's daughter, and his brother, his father, and his paternal uncle.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, in the narration of Abu Sulayman al-Jawzajani, said: The *akhtan* of a man are the husbands of his daughters, his sisters, his paternal aunts, his maternal aunts, and every woman who is *mahram* to him. His *asman* are every relative who is *mahram* to his wife.

Al-Nahhas said: In this matter, the more appropriate view concerning the *asman* is what al-Asma'i said, and that it comes from both sides together. It is said *sahartu al-shay'*, meaning I mixed it, so each of the two has mixed with the other.

The more appropriate view concerning the *akhtan* is what Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said, for two reasons. The first is a *marfu'* hadith. Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn Qusayt, from Muhammad ibn Usama ibn Zayd, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "As for you, O 'Ali, you are my *khatn* (son-in-law), the father of my children, and you are from me and I am from you." This indicates that the husband of a daughter is a *khatn*. The second reason is that the derivation of *khatn* is from *khatanahu*, meaning he cut it off, as though the husband has been cut off from his family, and has cut his wife off from her family.

Al-Dahhak said: *Sihr* is kinship through nursing. Ibn 'Atiyya said: In my view this is an error, caused by Ibn 'Abbas's statement: "Seven are prohibited by *nasab*, and five by *sihr*." In another narration: "Seven by *sihr*," meaning Allah's words, "Prohibited to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brother's daughters, and your sister's daughters" (4:23). This is the *nasab*. Then by *sihr* he means Allah's words, "And your mothers who nursed you" (4:23), up to His words, "and that you combine two sisters" (4:23). Then He mentioned the married women (*al-muhsanat*). The meaning of this is that Ibn 'Abbas intended: five are prohibited by *sihr* along with what was mentioned with it. By what he mentioned he pointed to its magnitude, which is *sihr*. Nursing is not *sihr*. Rather, nursing is the counterpart of *nasab*: whatever is prohibited by *nasab* is prohibited by nursing, according to the established hadith on this. Whoever narrated "five are prohibited by *sihr*" dropped from the two verses the combining of two sisters and the married women, who are women with husbands.

I say: Ibn 'Atiyya made nursing, together with what preceded, a form of *nasab*, and this is the view of al-Zajjaj. Abu Ishaq said: The *nasab* that is not *sihr* is from His words, "Prohibited to you are your mothers" up to "and that you combine two sisters." *Sihr* is the one who may marry you.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-Zahrawi related a view that *nasab* is through the sons, and *sihr* is through the daughters. I say: al-Nahhas also mentioned this view and said: because in-law relationship can come from two directions.

Ibn Sirin said: This verse was revealed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, because both *nasab* and *sihr* gathered them together.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Their union is a bond of prohibition until the Day of Resurrection.

**﴿And your Lord is ever Competent﴾** over the creation of whatever He wills.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that which neither benefits them nor harms them﴾. When He had enumerated the favours and demonstrated the perfection of His power, He marvelled at the polytheists in their associating with Him that which has no power to benefit or harm. That is, Allah is the One who created what He has mentioned, and yet these people, out of their ignorance, worship besides Him dead, inanimate objects that neither benefit nor harm.

(﴿And the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord﴾) It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that "the disbeliever" here is Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him, and its explanation is that he seeks support through the worship of idols against his allies. 'Ikrimah said: "the disbeliever" is Iblis, who showed support in his enmity toward his Lord. Mutarrif said: "the disbeliever" here is the Shaytan. Al-Hasan said: "zahiran" means a helper of Shaytan in acts of disobedience. It has also been said: the meaning is, the disbeliever was ever insignificant and humiliated before his Lord, having no worth or weight in His sight, from the Arab saying: "I put him behind my back (zahartu bihi)", meaning, I made him behind your back and did not turn to him. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs (zihriyyan)﴾, meaning, insignificant.

From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq: "Tamim ibn Qays, let not my need be cast behind the back, lest its answer be hard for me." This is the meaning of the statement of Abu 'Ubaydah. And "zahir" in the sense of "mazhur" (cast aside): the disbelief of the disbelievers is insignificant to Allah, exalted is He, and Allah holds it in contempt, because their disbelief does not harm Him. It has also been said: "And the disbeliever was ever against his Lord," meaning the idol he worships, which is strong and dominant, doing with him whatever it wills, because the inanimate has no power to repel harm or bring benefit.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 56–57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾. He means: a bringer of good tidings of Paradise and a warner from the Fire. And We have not sent you as a guardian over them, nor as one who compels them.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾. He means: for what I have brought you of the Qur'an and the revelation. The "min" (مِنْ) here is for emphasis (li-l-ta'kid).

﴿Except for whoever wills﴾. The meaning is: but whoever wills, so this is an exception of disconnection (istithna' munqati'), and the meaning is: but whoever wills ﴿to take a path to his Lord﴾, by spending from his wealth in the way of Allah; so let him spend. It is also permissible for it to be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), with an omitted modifier (hadhf al-mudaf) estimated: the sense being, "except the reward of whoever wills to take a path to his Lord," by following my religion, so that he may attain the honour of this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 56–57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾. He means: a bringer of good tidings of Paradise and a warner from the Fire. And We have not sent you as a guardian over them, nor as one who compels them.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾. He means: for what I have brought you of the Qur'an and the revelation. The "min" (مِنْ) here is for emphasis (li-l-ta'kid).

﴿Except for whoever wills﴾. The meaning is: but whoever wills, so this is an exception of disconnection (istithna' munqati'), and the meaning is: but whoever wills ﴿to take a path to his Lord﴾, by spending from his wealth in the way of Allah; so let him spend. It is also permissible for it to be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), with an omitted modifier (hadhf al-mudaf) estimated: the sense being, "except the reward of whoever wills to take a path to his Lord," by following my religion, so that he may attain the honour of this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 58:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And put your trust in the Living One who does not die﴾. The meaning of tawakkul (reliance) has already been explained in Surat Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 189, first or second edition.]], and in this surah. It is the heart's dependence upon Allah Exalted in all matters, and that means (ordinary) causes are intermediaries which He has commanded, without relying upon them.

(﴿And glorify Him with His praise﴾), i.e., declare Allah Exalted far above what these disbelievers attribute to Him of partners. Tasbih (glorifying) means tanzih (declaring Allah free of imperfection), and this has already been mentioned. It has also been said: "﴿And glorify Him﴾" means pray to Him, for prayer is called tasbih.

(﴿And sufficient is He as one who is All-Aware of the sins of His servants﴾), i.e., knowing, so He will recompense them for them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 59:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them in six days; then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ has already been discussed in Al-A'raf [see vol. 7, p. 218 onward]. And "Who" (alladhi) is in the genitive position as an attribute (na't) of "the Living" (al-Hayy). He said "between them" (baynahuma) and did not say "between them" (baynahunna), because He meant the two kinds, the two types and the two things, like the saying of al-Qutami: "Did it not grieve you that the ropes of Qays and Taghlib have been severed, becoming separated?" He meant "and the ropes of Taghlib," so He used the dual, while "al-hibal" (ropes) is a plural noun, because He meant the two things and the two types.

﴿The Most Merciful, so ask about Him one who is informed﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "ask about Him." A group of lexicographers have also reported that the ba' (ب) can carry the meaning of 'an (عن), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that is to befall﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 278]. And the poet said:

"Why did you not ask the horses, O daughter of Malik, if you are ignorant of what you did not know?"

And [Alqamah ibn 'Abadah] [In the manuscripts of the original: "Imru' al-Qays said", which is an error. The verse is from an ode of Alqamah, whose opening is: "A heart that is captivated by the beautiful women has yearned for you, after youth, when gray hair has come"]:

"If you ask me about women, then I am informed [in another narration: "perceptive", i.e., knowing] of the ailments of women and a physician."

That is, "about women and about what you did not know." 'Ali ibn Sulayman denied this and said: scholars of reasoning deny that the ba' can mean 'an, because this corrupts the meanings of the Arabs' saying: "If you met so-and-so, the lion would meet you with him," i.e., the lion would meet you through your meeting him. The meaning is: "ask with your asking him, one who is informed." Likewise Ibn Jubayr said: "the informed one" (al-khabir) is Allah, exalted is He. So "khabiran" is in the accusative as the object of the verb "ask."

I say: al-Zajjaj's view can be understood in a good way, namely that "the informed one" is other than Allah, i.e., "ask about Him one who is informed," meaning one who knows about Him, i.e., about His attributes and names. It has also been said: the meaning is "ask for Him an informed one," so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) from the implied pronoun. Al-Mahdawi said: it is not good as a circumstantial, since the circumstantial must be either from the questioner or from the one asked about, and it cannot be from the doer (the questioner), because the informed one has no need to ask another; nor can it be from the object, because the one asked about, the Most Merciful, is always informed, whereas circumstantials generally change and shift; unless it is understood as an emphatic circumstantial, like: ﴿And it is the truth, confirming﴾ [see vol. 2, p. 29], in which case it is permissible.

As for "al-Rahman," there are three possibilities in its case: it may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "established." It may be in the nominative with the meaning "He is the Most Merciful." It may be in the nominative as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "so ask about Him one who is informed." It is also permissible to read it in the genitive, meaning "and rely upon the Living who does not die, the Most Merciful," as an attribute. It is also permissible to read it in the accusative as a praise (madh).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 60:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful,"﴾ i.e., to Allah, exalted is He.

(They say, "And what is the Most Merciful?") in a manner of denial and astonishment, meaning: "We do not know the Most Merciful except the Rahman of al-Yamamah," by which they meant Musaylimah the liar. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi claimed that they were only ignorant of the attribute, not of the one described by it, and he based this on their saying "And what is the Most Merciful?" and not "And who is the Most Merciful?" Ibn al-Hassar said: "It seems that he, may Allah have mercy on him, did not read the other verse: ﴿and they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾" [[see vol. 9, p. 317]].

(Shall we prostrate to what you command us?) This is the reading of the people of Madinah and Basra, meaning: to what you, O Muhammad, command us. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred it. Al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yamurunā" with the letter ya', meaning the Most Merciful. Abu 'Ubayd interpreted it thus, saying: "Had they acknowledged that the Most Merciful had commanded them, they would not have been disbelievers." Al-Nahhas said: "It is not necessary to interpret the reading of the Kufans with this far-fetched interpretation. Rather, the better interpretation is that they meant 'to what the Prophet ﷺ commands us,' and the reading is valid on this basis, although the first is clearer and closer in meaning."

(And it increases them in aversion.) i.e., the saying of the one who says to them, "Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful," increases them in aversion from the religion. Sufyan al-Thawri used to say concerning this verse: "My God, the more it increases them in aversion, the more it increases me in submission to You."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 61:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations (buruj)﴾, meaning mansions (manazil). Their mention has already preceded [[See vol. 10, p. 9.]].

(And placed therein a lamp (siraj)): Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the sun. Its parallel is His saying: "and made the sun a lamp" [[See vol. 19, p. 305.]]. The reading of the majority is "siraj" in the singular. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "surujan" (سُرُجًا), meaning the great, blazing stars. The first reading is preferred by Abu 'Ubayd, because he interpreted the surujs as stars and the buruj as stars, so the meaning comes out as stars and stars. al-Nahhas said: but the interpretation for them is that Aban ibn Taghlib said: the surujs are the stars, the shining ones (al-darari). al-Tha'labi said: like Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, the two Simak stars, and the like.

(And a moon (qamaran) giving light): it gives light to the earth when it rises. 'Isma related from al-A'mash "wa-qumran" (وَقُمْرًا) with a damma on the qaf and sukun on the mim. This is a shadh (irregular) reading, and even if there were nothing against it except that Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who was the imam of the Muslims in his time, said: "Do not write down what 'Isma, the one who transmits the readings, reports," and Abu Hatim al-Sijistani was very fond of mentioning what this 'Isma reports.

In it there are four issues.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿khilfatan (in succession)﴾. Abu Ubayda said: *al-khilfah* is everything that comes after something else. Each of the night and the day succeeds the other. It is said of one with a gastric ailment: "He has been afflicted with *khilfah*," meaning standing and sitting alternating, one replacing the other. From this comes the *khilfat al-nabat* (the second growth of plants), which is the leaf that emerges after the first leaves in summer. Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said in this sense:

*Herds of wild cattle and gazelles walk there in succession,*
*and their young rise up from every resting place.* [[*Al-ayn* is the plural of *a'yan* and *ayna*, meaning wild cattle, named for the largeness of their eyes. *Al-atla'* is the plural of *tala*, meaning the young of the cow and the young of the gazelle. *Al-majthim* is the place where they rest, that is, where they are made to stand.]]

*Al-reem* is the young of the gazelle, its plural being *aram*. He means: when one group departs, another group comes. From this is the saying of another, who described a woman who moved regularly from a dwelling in winter to a dwelling in summer. [[He is Yazid ibn Mu'awiya. *Al-Matrun* is a place in Syria near Damascus.]]

*She has with al-Matrun, when*
*the ants have eaten what they had gathered,*
*a succession, until, when she settles in spring,*
*she dwells from Jallaq in churches*

*In houses in the midst of a monastery,*
*around which the olives have ripened.*

Mujahid said: "*khilfatan*" is from *al-khilaf* (difference): this one is white and this one is black. The first meaning is stronger. It was also said: they alternate in light and darkness, in increase and decrease. It was also said that this is an elision of a modifier, meaning: He made the night and the day possessors of succession, that is, of alternation.

﴿لِمَنْ أَرَادَ أَنْ يَذَّكَّرَ﴾ [for whoever wishes to take heed] means: *yatadhakkar*, that is, he remembers, so that he knows that God did not make it thus in vain, and so he reflects upon God's created things, and thanks God for His blessings upon him in reason, thought and understanding. Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan said: its meaning is that whoever misses something of good at night makes it up by day, and whoever misses it by day makes it up at night. In the Sahih: "There is no person who has a prayer at night and sleep overcomes him from it, but that he prays between sunrise and the midday prayer, except that God records for him the reward of his prayer, and his sleep becomes a charity for him." Muslim related from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sleeps through his portion [of recitation] or part of it, and then recites it between the dawn prayer and the midday prayer, it is recorded for him as though he had recited it at night."

The second issue: Ibn al-Arabi said: I heard Dhu al-Shahid al-Akbar say: God created the servant living and knowing, and by this is his perfection. He subjected him to the affliction of sleep, the necessity of excretion, and the deficiency of creation, since perfection belongs only to the First, the Creator. So whatever enables a man to repel sleep by eating little and staying awake in obedience to God, let him do it. It is a great loss for a man to live sixty years, sleeping through its nights, so that half of his life is lost in vanity, and sleeping a sixth of the day for rest, so that two-thirds of it is lost, and there remains for him twenty years of life. And it is ignorance and folly for a man to waste two-thirds of his life in a fleeting pleasure, and not to spend his life in staying awake for a lasting pleasure with the Self-Sufficient, the Faithful, who is neither destitute nor unjust.

The third issue: things do not differ in themselves, for substances and accidents are alike in terms of existence, and distinction occurs only through attributes. It has been disputed which of the two times is better, the night or the day. In fasting there is sufficient indication of the matter, and God knows best, as Ibn al-Arabi said. I say: the night is of great rank. God commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to stand in it, saying: ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory prayer for you﴾, and ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night﴾, as will come with its explanation. He praised the believers for standing in it, saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire, and a man's prayer in the depth of the night, and in it there is an hour in which supplication is answered, and in it the Lord, blessed and exalted, descends," as will come with its explanation, God willing.

The fourth issue: Hamzah alone recited *yadhkur* with a sukun on the dhal and a damma on the kaf [*yadhkur*]. This is the recitation (*qira'ah*) of Ibn Wathhab, Talhah and al-Nakha'i. In the codex (*mushaf*) of Ubayy it is *yatadhakkar*, with an added ta'. The rest recited *yadhdhakkar*, with a shadda on the kaf. *Yadhkur* and *yadhdhakkar* have one meaning. It was also said: the meaning of *yadhkur* with the light form is that he remembers what he forgot at one of the two times at the other time, or so that he remembers the glorification and praise of God in them.

﴿أَوْ أَرَادَ شُكُوراً﴾ [or wishes to be thankful]. It is said: *shakara yashkuru shukran wa shukuran*, like *kafara yakfuru kufran wa kufuran*. This *shukur* is on the basis that they made the two [night and day] a support for their livelihood. And it is as if, when they said: ﴿And what is the Most Merciful?﴾, they said: He is the One who is able to do these things.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 25, verse 63:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾. When He mentioned the ignorance of the polytheists and their slander against the Qur'an and prophethood, He also mentioned His believing servants and described their qualities. He attributed them to His servanthood as an honour for them, as in His saying: "Glory be to the One who took His servant by night" (17:1). This has already been discussed (see vol. 10, p. 205 of the original edition). Whoever obeys Allah, worships Him, and occupies his hearing, sight, tongue and heart with what He has commanded, is the one who truly deserves the name of servanthood. Whoever is the opposite of this is covered by His saying: ﴿They are like cattle; nay, they are further astray﴾ (7:179), meaning in failing to take heed, as has been discussed in "al-A'raf" (see vol. 7, p. 324 onward of the original edition).

It is as if He said: "The servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth," and the word "hum" (they) has been omitted, as in your saying: "Zayd the commander" (meaning) "Zayd is the commander." Thus "alladhina" (those who) is the predicate of an omitted subject; this is the view of al-Akhfash. It has also been said that the predicate is His saying at the end of the surah: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the high chamber for their patience﴾ (25:75). What lies between the subject and the predicate are their attributes and what is connected to them; this is the view of al-Zajjaj. He said: "It is also permissible for the predicate to be ﴿those who walk upon the earth﴾." "Yamshuna" (they walk) is an expression for their living, the duration of their lives, and their conduct. He mentioned from this the greatest part, especially since walking on the earth involves moving among people, mixing and associating with them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿hawnan﴾ (in humility). "Al-hawn" is the verbal noun of "al-hayyin" (the gentle, calm), and it derives from tranquillity and dignity. In the tafsir it is said: they walk upon the earth as forbearing and humble people, walking with moderation. Moderation, deliberateness, and good bearing are among the characteristics of prophethood. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O people, adopt tranquillity, for righteousness does not lie in haste" (al-idla'). [*Al-iydaa': a pace like the trot (khabab).*] It is also narrated in his description (ﷺ) that when he moved, he moved with vigour (taqal'ul), and he stepped forward with a forward inclination (takaffu'), and he walked with calm (hawnan), long of stride; when he walked, it was as if he were descending from a slope. "Taqal'ul" means lifting the foot with force; "takaffu'" means leaning toward the proper manner and direction of walking. "Al-hawn" means gentleness and dignity. "Al-dhari'" means one with wide steps, meaning that in his walk he lifted his foot quickly and extended his stride, unlike the walk of the arrogant, and he aimed at a dignified bearing, all of it with gentleness and composure, without haste. As he said: "as if he were descending from a slope," as reported by Qadi 'Iyad.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) used to walk quickly by natural disposition, not by affectation. Al-Zuhri said: "Hastening in walking removes the radiance of the face." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He means rapid, hurried haste, because it undermines dignity; the good lies in moderation." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "I used to ask about the tafsir of His saying, may He be exalted: 'Those who walk upon the earth in humility,' and I found no cure in it. Then I saw in a dream someone who came to me and said: 'They are those who do not wish to cause corruption on the earth.'" Al-Qushayri said: "It has also been said: they do not walk for corruption or disobedience, but in obedience to Allah and in permissible matters, without vanity." Allah, may He be exalted, has also said: ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly; indeed, Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾ (17:37). (See vol. 14, p. 69 onward of the original edition.)

Ibn 'Abbas said: "[They walk] in obedience, in what is good, and in humility." Al-Hasan said: "They are forbearing: if someone behaves ignorantly toward them, they do not respond with ignorance." It has also been said: "They do not behave arrogantly toward people."

I say: all these meanings are close to one another, and what unites them is knowledge of Allah, fear of Him, knowledge of His rulings, and awe of His punishment and retribution. May Allah make us among them by His grace and kindness.

A group held that "hawnan" is connected to His saying "walk upon the earth," meaning that walking itself is "hawn." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It seems that this may be interpreted to mean that the character of the one who walks is gentle and appropriate to his walking, so the meaning returns to what we have explained. As for the meaning being the attribute of walking alone, it is false, for many a person walks gently and calmly while being a sleek wolf (dhi'b atlas)." [*Al-atlas among wolves is one whose fur has fallen out, and it is the most cunning kind. It was also said: it is one whose colour is tinged with grey shading toward black.*] The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to walk with a forward inclination, as if he were descending from a slope. He, peace and blessings be upon him, is the chief (al-sadr) of this community. As for his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever among you walks in greed, let him walk slowly" (hadith), he meant it regarding the state of the heart and not walking alone. Do you not see that the false ones who adorn themselves with religion adopted only the outward form of walking, until the poet said in censure of them:

"All of them walk slowly... all of them seek prey."

[*This is from the words of Abu Ja'far al-Mansur the caliph in praise of 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, the well-known ascetic. Its completion is: "Except 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd."*]

I say: In its opposite, Ibn al-'Arabi recited for himself:

"I was humble though my lineage is noble, and I won the prize of the race through gentleness in the matter.
A calm that has no base in the corruption of the inner self; and most of people's calm comes from the greatness of pride."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say: "Peace"﴾. Al-Nahhas said: "'Salaman' (peace) is not from 'taslim' (greeting) but from 'taslum' (being safe from), as the Arabs say: 'salaman,' meaning 'safety from you,' that is, freedom from you." It is in the accusative under one of two possibilities: it may be governed by "qalu" (they said), or it may be a verbal noun (masdar); this is the view of Sibawayh. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "What I say is that 'qalu' is the governing verb of 'salaman,' because the meaning is 'they said this utterance.'" Mujahid said: "The meaning of 'salaman' is 'sound words' (sadadan)." That is, one says to the ignorant a word by which one turns him away gently and softly. On this interpretation, "qalu" governs "salaman" according to the method of the grammarians, since it has the sense of "qawlan" (speech).

A group said: the one addressed should say to the ignorant "salaman" with this word, meaning "we greet you with a greeting" or "greeting," and the like; so the governing verb would be a verb from its own root, according to the method of the grammarians.

Issue: This verse came before the verse of the sword. Some of its ruling concerning the unbelievers was abrogated (naskh), and its courtesy remained for the Muslims until the Day of Resurrection. Sibawayh mentioned abrogation regarding this verse in his book, and he spoke of no other abrogation; he preferred that the intended meaning is "salamah" (safety) and not "taslim" (greeting), because the believers were never commanded to greet the unbelievers. The verse is Meccan, and the verse of the sword abrogated it. Al-Nahhas said: "We know of no statement by Sibawayh on the meaning of abrogation and abrogated except in this verse." Sibawayh said: "The Muslims were not commanded at that time to greet the polytheists, but it is in the sense of His saying: 'safety from you, and there is neither good nor evil between us and you.'" Al-Mubarrad said: "It should have been said: the Muslims were not commanded at that time to fight them; then they were commanded to fight them." Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "Sibawayh erred in this and expressed it badly." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The Muslims were not commanded at that time to greet the polytheists, nor were they forbidden from it; rather they were commanded to forgive and to turn away graciously. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would stand at their gatherings, greet them, draw near to them, and would not flatter them." People agree that if a foolish believer treats you harshly, it is permissible for you to say to him: "Peace be upon you."

I say: This view is more consistent with the evidences of the Sunnah. We have explained in the surah of "Maryam" (see vol. 11, p. 111 onward of the original edition) the scholars' disagreement over the permissibility of greeting unbelievers. So there is no need to claim abrogation. And Allah knows best.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl mentioned, saying: Al-Khalil narrated to me: "I came to Abu Rabi'a al-A'rabi, who was among the most knowledgeable people I had seen. He was on a roof, and when we greeted him, he returned the greeting and said to us: 'Istawu' (rise up/level yourselves). We remained perplexed and did not know what he meant. A Bedouin beside him said to us: 'He has commanded you to rise up.'" Al-Khalil said: "It is from the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿Then He rose over the heaven, and it was smoke﴾ (41:11). So we climbed up to him. He said: 'Would you like some leavened bread, milk, and flowing water?' We said: 'Now,' and we parted from him. He said: 'Salaman.' We did not know what he meant." He (the narrator) said: "The Bedouin said: 'He asked you for a mutual leaving with neither good nor evil in it.'" Al-Khalil said: "It is from the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say: 'Peace'﴾."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I saw in some histories that Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi, who leaned toward 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), said one day in the presence of al-Ma'mun, with a group present: 'I used to see 'Ali ibn Abi Talib in dreams, and I would say to him: "Who are you?" He would say: "'Ali ibn Abi Talib." I would go with him to a bridge, and he would go ahead of me in crossing it. I would say: "You claim this matter through a woman, and we have more right to it than you."' I did not see in his answer the eloquence that is reported of him." Al-Ma'mun said: "And how did he answer you?" He said: "He would say to me: 'Salaman.'" The narrator said: "It seems Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi did not remember the verse, or it had slipped from his mind at that moment." Al-Ma'mun alerted those present to the verse and said: "By Allah, O uncle, it is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and he answered you with the most eloquent answer." So Ibrahim was humiliated and felt shame. And it was a vision that was undoubtedly true.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 64:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Bāta (to spend the night) is said of a man when the night overtakes him, whether he sleeps or does not sleep." Zuhayr said [[In the manuscript of the original: "Imru' al-Qays said." This is a mistake. The verse is from a qasida of Zuhayr whose opening line is:

Ṣaḥā al-qalb ʿan Salmā wa-aqṣara bāṭiluhu ... wa-ʿarā afrāsa al-ṣibā wa-rawāḥilahu]]:

"So we spent the night standing beside the heads of our horses,
Each of us struggling with it, and it struggling with us."

They also recited, describing the saints:

"Prevent your eyelids from tasting sleep,
and pour out tears streaming down the cheeks.
Know that you are mortal and will be held to account,
O you who have remained under the displeasure of the Majestic.

For God there are a people who sincerely devoted themselves to His love,
so He was pleased with them and chose them as servants.

A people who, when darkness covers them,
spend the night there prostrating and standing.

Lean of belly from abstinence, slender,
knowing no food but what is lawful."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Whoever prays two rakʿas or more after the ʿIshāʾ prayer has spent the night prostrating and standing before God." Al-Kalbi said: "Whoever performs two rakʿas after Maghrib and four after ʿIshāʾ has spent the night prostrating and standing."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 65–66:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell"﴾. That is, they are, along with their obedience, fearful, apprehensive and anxious of the punishment of Allah. Ibn 'Abbas said: they say that in their prostration and their standing (in prayer).

(Indeed, its punishment was ever a constant burden) That is, binding, perpetual, never separating. From this the creditor (al-gharim) is so named because of his persistence. It is said: "So-and-so is mughram with such-and-such," meaning he is bound to it and devoted to it. This is its meaning in the speech of the Arabs, as mentioned by Ibn al-A'rabi, Ibn 'Arafa and others. Al-A'sha said:

If He punishes, it will be a constant burden, and if He gives abundantly, He does not care.

Al-Hasan said: They know that every creditor separates from his debtor, except the creditor of Hell. Al-Zajjaj said: al-gharam is the most severe punishment. Ibn Zayd said: al-gharam is evil. Abu 'Ubayda said: destruction. The meaning is one. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: Allah, may He be exalted, demanded from them the price of the blessings in this world, and they did not bring it, so He charged them its price by casting them into the Fire.

(Indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and a station) That is, how wretched is the place of settlement and how wretched is the station. That is, they say this out of knowledge, and when they say it out of knowledge, they are more aware of the great worth of what they seek, and that is closer to being granted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 65–66:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell"﴾. That is, they are, along with their obedience, fearful, apprehensive and anxious of the punishment of Allah. Ibn 'Abbas said: they say that in their prostration and their standing (in prayer).

(Indeed, its punishment was ever a constant burden) That is, binding, perpetual, never separating. From this the creditor (al-gharim) is so named because of his persistence. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 67:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾. The exegetes differed concerning the interpretation of this verse. Al-Nahhas said: Among the best of what has been said about its meaning is that whoever spends in other than obedience to Allah, that is extravagance (israf), and whoever withholds from obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that is niggardliness (iqtar), and whoever spends in obedience to Allah, the Exalted, that is balance (qawam).

Ibn 'Abbas said: Whoever spends a hundred thousand in what is right is not extravagant, and whoever spends a dirham in other than its right is extravagant, and whoever withholds what is due upon him has been niggardly. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and others said the same. 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah said: Extravagance is that you spend the wealth of another. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This and similar views are not connected with the verse. The correct view is that spending in disobedience is something the Shari'ah has forbidden, whether little or much, and likewise transgressing upon the property of others, and these described people are far removed from that. The discipline in this verse concerns spending on acts of obedience within what is permissible. The Shari'ah's guidance in this is that a person should not be so lavish that he wastes another right or his dependants and the like, nor should he be so restrictive and stingy that he starves his dependants and goes to excess in miserliness. The good in this matter is balance (qawam), that is, moderation, and the balance differs for each person according to his dependants and his condition, his lightness of burden, his patience and his endurance in earning, or the opposite of these qualities. The best of matters is their middle course. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ allowed Abu Bakr al-Siddiq to give away all his wealth in charity, because that was a middle course relative to his endurance and patience in religion, and he forbade others from doing so. And Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said well: It is the one who does not let himself go hungry, nor leave himself naked, and does not spend such that people say he has been extravagant. Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: They are those who do not wear clothes for beauty, and do not eat food for pleasure. Yazid also said concerning this verse: Those were the companions of Muhammad ﷺ; they did not eat food for luxury and pleasure, nor wear clothes for beauty, but they desired from food only what would stave off their hunger and strengthen them to worship their Lord, and from clothing only what would cover their nakedness and shield them from heat and cold. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz when he married him his daughter Fatimah: What is your expenditure? 'Umar said to him: A good deed between two bad ones, and then he recited this verse. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: It is enough of extravagance for a man that he should desire something and buy it and eat it. In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, it is extravagance that you eat everything you desire." Abu 'Ubaydah said: They did not exceed what is proper, nor were they miserly, like His saying, may He be exalted: "And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched." The poet said: "And do not go to excess in any matter, but be moderate; both extremes of the matter are blameworthy." Another said:

When a man gives his soul everything it desires... and does not restrain it, it yearns for every falsehood,

And drives it toward sin and shame, by means of the sweetness of a fleeting pleasure to which it calls it.

'Umar said to his son 'Asim: O my son, eat until half your belly is full, do not discard a garment until you have patched it, and do not be among a people who place what Allah has provided them in their bellies and on their backs. And Hatim al-Ta'i said:

When you give your belly its desire, and your private part too, both attain the furthest limit of blame.

(And they were not niggardly, وَلَمْ يَقْتُرُوا) Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash, 'Asim and Yahya ibn Wththab, according to a variant from them, read "yaqturu" with a fathah on the ya and a dammah on the ta, and this is a good reading, from qatara yaqturu. This is the analogical form for an intransitive verb, like qa'ada yaq'udu. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Ibn Kathir read with a fathah on the ya and a kasrah on the ta, and this is a well-known and good dialect. The people of Madinah, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read with a dammah on the ya and a kasrah on the ta. Al-Tha'labi said: All of these are sound dialects. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Hatim was surprised at the reading of the people of Madinah, because in his view no irregular reading occurs in their recitation; it is only said "aqtara yuqtiru" when one becomes poor, as He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "And upon the one of limited means is his measure." Abu Hatim interpreted it for them as meaning that the extravagant person quickly becomes poor. This is a distant interpretation. Rather, the interpretation for them is that Abu 'Umar al-Jarmi related from al-Asma'i that it is said of a person when he restricts: qatara yaqturu and yaqtaru, and aqtara yuqtiru. On this basis the reading is valid, although the fathah on the ya is more sound, closer in meaning, more famous and better known. Abu 'Amr and the people read "qawaman" with a fathah on the qaf, meaning moderation. Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read "qiwaman" with a kasrah on the qaf, meaning a limit, a firm standard, and the settled condition of a matter. The qiwam with a kasrah is what a matter continues upon and becomes stable in. The two are dialects with the same meaning. "Qawaman" is the predicate of "kana," and its subject is implied within it, meaning that spending was moderation between extravagance and restriction; this is what al-Farra' said. He had another view which makes "bayna" the subject of "kana" and puts it in the accusative, because these expressions are used often, so they were left in their form in the position of nominative. Al-Nahhas said: I do not know what the basis of this is, because "bayna," when it is in the position of nominative, is made nominative, as one says: "bayna 'aynayhi ahmar" (between his eyes is red).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 68–69:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity﴾ is a separation of His believing servants from the attributes of the disbelievers in their worship of idols, their killing of souls by burying daughters alive, and other forms of injustice, assassination, raids, and fornication, which was permissible among them. One of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) who turned this verse away from its apparent sense said: it is not fitting for those whom the Most Merciful has attributed to Himself with the attribution of special distinction, and whom He has mentioned and described with the qualities of recognition and honour, that these abominable acts should occur from them, so that they would be praised for their negation, because they are higher and more noble. So he said: its meaning is that they do not take desire as a deity, and they do not humiliate themselves with sins, which would be a killing of themselves. The meaning of "except by right" is: except with the knife of patience and the sword of striving, so they do not look upon women who are not lawful to them with lust, which would be illicit intercourse, but only out of necessity, which would be like marriage.

Our shaykh Abu al-'Abbas said: this is a pleasing speech, but upon examination it is faulty. It is a esoteric (batiniyya) origin and a vain (batiliyya) tendency. The honouring of Allah's servants through the special attribution is only valid after they have adorned themselves with those praiseworthy qualities and emptied themselves of the opposites of those blameworthy attributes. Thus He began in the opening of these verses with the qualities of adornment (tahalli) as an honouring of them, then followed them with the qualities of emptying (takhalli) as a distancing from their opposites. And Allah knows best.

I say: among what demonstrates the falsehood of what this speaker claims, that those matters are not to be taken in their apparent sense, is what Muslim narrated from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, which sin is greatest in the sight of Allah?" He said: "That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that he will share your food." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with the wife of your neighbour." So Allah the Exalted revealed its confirmation: "And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, and do not commit fornication; and whoever does that will meet a penalty (athām)."

And athām in the speech of the Arabs means punishment, and Ibn Zayd and Qatadah read this verse with that meaning.

From this is the poet's saying: "May Allah recompense Ibn 'Urwa, since he has become disobedient, and disobedience has for him a penalty (athām)," i.e., recompense and punishment.

'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: "athām" is a valley in Hell which Allah made a punishment for the disbelievers. The poet said: "You met the destructions in our war, and after the destructions you will meet athām." Al-Suddi said: it is a mountain in it. He said: "And our station was that we invoked against them at Abtah of Dhu al-Majaz, which has athām."

In Sahih Muslim also, from Ibn 'Abbas: some people among the polytheists had killed much and committed fornication much, then they came to Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: "What you say and call to is indeed good, and you inform us that for what we have done there is an expiation." So there was revealed: "And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, and do not commit fornication; and whoever does that will meet a penalty." And there was revealed: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves..." up to the end of the verse. It has been said that this verse, "O My servants who have transgressed," was revealed concerning Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn 'Abbas. Its explanation will come in "al-Zumar."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except by right﴾ means: by that which makes it right that souls be killed for, such as disbelief after belief or adultery after being married (ihsan), as has been explained earlier in "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 133, first or second edition.]].

(And they do not commit fornication) so they make lawful the private parts without marriage or ownership by right of the right hand. This verse indicates that after disbelief there is nothing greater than killing a soul without right, then fornication. For this reason, the punishment for fornication is established as death for one who is married (muhsan), or flogging for one who is not married.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty (athām). The punishment will be doubled for him﴾ — Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yud'af" (will be doubled), and "yakhlud" (will abide) in the jussive. Ibn Kathir read "yuda''af" with a doubled ayn and the alif dropped, and with the jussive in "yud'af" and "yakhlud". Talhah ibn Sulayman read "nud'if" with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the doubled ayn; "al-'adhab" is in the accusative, and "yakhlud" is jussive; this is the reading of Abu Ja'far and Shaybah.

'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read "yudā'afu" and "yakhludu" with raf' in both, on the basis of coordination (al-'atf) and resumption (al-isti'naf). Talhah ibn Sulayman read "wa-takhludu" with ta', addressing the disbeliever. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr "wa-yukhladu" with a damma on the yā' from below and a fatha on the lam; Abu 'Ali said: this is an error from the point of transmission. "Yud'af" in the jussive is a substitute (badal) for "yalqa", which is the answer of the conditional. Sibawayh said: the doubling of the punishment is the meeting of the penalty. The poet said: "Whenever you come to us and visit us in our homes, you will find firewood thick and a fire blazing." Another said: "Indeed upon me is Allah, that you will pledge allegiance, [[The evidence lies in the taking of "tubāya'" as a substitute for "tubāya'a" (by a reading) and its replacement. He meant by "Allah" — the meaning being "upon me and Allah" — so when the particle was dropped the accusative was used.]] you will be taken by force or you will come willingly." As for the raf', there are two views: one is that you separate it from what precedes; the other is that it is taken as carried upon the meaning, as if a speaker said: what is the meeting of the penalty? It was said to him: the punishment will be doubled for him.

And (muhānan) means: humiliated, abject, distanced, rejected.

[Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 25, verse 70]

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous work﴾. There is no disagreement among the scholars that the exception applies to the disbeliever and the fornicator. They differed regarding the Muslim murderer, as its explanation has already preceded in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 332 and following, first or second edition.]]. And the discussion of the permissibility of delaying the exception (istithna') in an oath has passed in "al-Ma'idah" [[See vol. 6, p. 273, first or second edition.]], and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, who used this verse as evidence.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Then those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾. Al-Nahhas said: Among the best that has been said about it is that a believer is written in place of a disbeliever, and an obedient one in place of a disobedient one. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: it means that Allah will replace for them shirk with faith. A similar report is narrated from al-Hasan. Al-Hasan said: Some people say the replacement is in the Hereafter, and that is not so; rather the replacement is in this world: Allah replaces for them faith in place of shirk, sincerity in place of doubt, and chastity in place of immorality. Al-Zajjaj said: It does not mean that good deeds are placed in the place of evil deeds, but that repentance is placed in the place of evil deeds, and good deeds come with repentance. Abu Dharr narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "That evil deeds are replaced with good deeds." A similar meaning is narrated from Salman al-Farisi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others. Abu Hurayrah said: That is in the Hereafter, for one whose good deeds outweigh his evil deeds, so Allah replaces the evil deeds with good deeds. And in a report: "Some people will wish that they had multiplied their evil deeds." It was said: Who are they? He said: "Those whose evil deeds Allah replaces with good deeds." Abu Hurayrah narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ); al-Tha'labi and al-Qushayri mentioned it. It was also said: "Replacement" is an expression for forgiveness, meaning that Allah forgives them those evil deeds, not that He replaces them with good deeds.

I say: It is not far-fetched, in the generosity of Allah, the Exalted, that when the servant's repentance is sound, He should place a good deed in the place of every evil deed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Mu'adh: "Follow the evil deed with a good deed, and it will erase it, and deal with people with good character." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I know the last of the people of Paradise to enter Paradise, and the last of the people of Hellfire to leave it: a man who will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: Present to him his minor sins and withhold from him his major sins. His minor sins will be presented to him, and it will be said: You did on such a day such and such, and on such a day such and such. He will say: Yes, and he cannot deny it, while he is fearful about his major sins being presented to him. It will be said to him: For you there is a good deed in place of every evil deed. He will say: O Lord, I have done things I do not see here." Then I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laugh until his molars showed.

Abu Tawil [[Abu Tawil: a kunya for Shatab al-Mudud, a man from Kindah.]] said: O Messenger of Allah, what do you think of a man who committed all sins and left none of them, and in that he did not leave any "hajjah" or "dajjah" without seizing it. Is there repentance for him? He said: "Have you embraced Islam?" He said: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, without partner, and I bear witness that you are the servant and messenger of Allah. He said: "Yes. You will do good deeds, and leave evil deeds; Allah will make all of them good deeds." He said: And my treacheries and my immoralities, O Prophet of Allah? He said: "Yes." He said: Allah is greatest! And he kept repeating it until he disappeared. Al-Tha'labi mentioned it. Mubashshir ibn 'Ubayd, who was knowledgeable in grammar and Arabic, said: The "hajjah" is what is cut off from the pilgrims when they set out, and the "dajjah" is what is cut off from them when they return.

(And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 71:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he turns back to Allah with a [sincere] turning.﴾ It is not said: "Whoever stands, then indeed he stands." So how does He say "whoever repents, then indeed he turns back"?

Ibn 'Abbas said: The meaning is: whoever of the people of Makkah believed and emigrated, and had not killed or committed fornication, but did righteous deeds and performed the obligatory duties, then indeed he turns back to Allah with a [proper] turning; that is, indeed I have advanced them and favoured them over those who fought the Prophet (ﷺ) and made lawful the things that are forbidden.

Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that the first verse concerns those who repent from among the polytheists, and for this reason He said: "except for those who repent and believe." Then there is joined to it those who repent from among the Muslims and follow their repentance with righteous deeds; for them too is the ruling of those who repent.

It was also said: that is, whoever repents with his tongue but does not actualize that by his action, that repentance is not beneficial. Rather, whoever repents and does righteous deeds, actualizing his repentance through righteous deeds, is the one who turns back to Allah with a [true] turning; that is, he repents with the true repentance, which is the sincere (nasuh) repentance. For this reason it is emphasized with the verbal noun (masdar). So "matāban" is a verbal noun whose meaning is emphasis, like His saying: "And Allah spoke to Musa with [real] speech" (takliman); that is, indeed he turns back to Allah truly, and Allah will truly accept his repentance.

In this there are two issues.

The first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾, meaning they do not attend falsehood and untruth, nor look on it. Al-zur (falsehood) is every false thing that has been made to look attractive and adorned, and the greatest of it is shirk (associating partners with God) and the exaltation of rivals (andad). This is how al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and Ibn 'Abbas explained it; and in one report from Ibn 'Abbas, it is the festivals of the polytheists. 'Ikrimah said: it is play that was done in the Jahiliyyah and called al-zur. Mujahid said: it is singing (ghina'), and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah also said this. Ibn Jurayj said: it is lying, and this was also narrated from Mujahid. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah and Muhammad ibn 'Ali said: the meaning is that they do not bear false witness (bi-l-zur), taken from shahadah (testimony) and not from mushahadah (witnessing).

Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for the view that it is lying, it is sound, because all of these return to lying. As for the one who said it is a play of the Jahiliyyah, that is forbidden when it involves gambling, ignorance, or a matter that leads back to disbelief. As for the view that it is singing, it does not reach this limit. I say: among singing there is that whose hearing reaches the level of prohibition, such as poems that describe beautiful figures, wine, and other things that stir up natures and take them out of moderation, or that arouse a hidden love of amusement, like the words of one of them:

"Golden of hue, from whose cheeks you would think fire is being struck,
Warn me of his disgrace, would that he came and I were exposed."

Especially when accompanied by shababat (a type of flute, with shaddah: a kind of wind instrument (mawlid)) and tarat (frame drums), as is done today in these times, as we have explained in another place.

As for the one who said it is false testimony, which is the second issue: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, used to flog a false witness forty lashes, blacken his face, shave his head, and parade him through the market. Most scholars said: his testimony is never accepted again, even if he repents and his condition becomes good; his affair is with Allah. It has also been said: if he was not notorious and his condition became good, his testimony is accepted, as has been explained earlier in the commentary on Surah al-Hajj [see vol. 12, p. 55 of the first or second edition]; so reflect on it there.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾. The discussion of al-laghw has already been given [see vol. 3, p. 99 ff. of the first or second edition]: it is every worthless thing of speech or action, so it includes singing, amusement and what is close to them, and it includes the foolishness of the polytheists, their harm to the believers, mention of women, and other evils. Mujahid said: when they are harmed, they overlook it. And it is narrated from him: when marriage is mentioned, they refrain from it. Al-Hasan said: al-laghw is all acts of disobedience, and this is comprehensive. And "kiraman" means turning away, disapproving, not being pleased with it, not colluding in it, and not sitting with its people.

That is, they pass by like noble people who do not enter into falsehood. It is said: so-and-so was honourable (takarrama) regarding what would disgrace him, meaning he kept himself pure and honoured himself from it. It is narrated that 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud heard singing, so he hurried away. This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed, the son of Umm 'Abd has become honourable." It has also been said: from passing by idle talk with dignity is to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 73:

There are two issues here.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord﴾, meaning: when the Qur'an is recited to them, they remember their Hereafter and their return, and they do not neglect it, to the point that they are like one who does not hear. And He said: (they do not fall down), though there is no falling involved, just as one says: "He sat weeping," even though he was not sitting. This was said by al-Tabari, and he chose it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "That they fall down deaf and blind is the attribute of the disbelievers, and it is an expression of their turning away. It is coupled with your saying: 'So-and-so sat cursing me' and 'So-and-so stood weeping,' while you did not intend to report a sitting or a standing; these are only preparatory expressions in speech and phrasing." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "So it is as if the one who listens to the reminder is upright of spine and sound in affair; when he turns away and goes astray, that is a falling (khurur), which is a collapse without order or arrangement, although the one who falls prostrate has been likened to it, but its origin is falling without order." It was also said: meaning, when the signs of Allah are recited to them, their hearts tremble, so they fall down prostrating and weeping, and they do not fall upon them deaf and blind. al-Farra' said: meaning, they do not remain in their former state as if they had not heard.

The second: Some scholars said: whoever hears a man recite a verse of prostration should prostrate with him, because he has heard the signs of Allah being recited to him. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is binding only on the reciter alone. As for others, it is not binding on them except in one case: if a man recites the Qur'an and recites the verse of prostration, then if the one sitting with him sits intending to listen, he should prostrate with him; but if he has not committed himself to listening along with him, there is no prostration upon him." This has already been discussed in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 359, first or second edition.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verse 74–77 (part 1 of 2):

Some said: he meant a'immah, just as the speaker says "these are our commander" meaning "our commanders." The poet said:
"O my blamers, do not increase my reproach; the blamers are not commanders over me,"
meaning, not commanders (umara'). His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the high chamber for what they endured﴾. What intervened between the subject and its predicate are their attributes of adornment and avoidance, and they are eleven: humility, forbearance, night prayer, fear, avoiding extravagance and stinginess, freedom from shirk, adultery and killing, repentance and avoiding lying, pardoning the offender, accepting admonitions, and supplication to Allah. Al-Dahhak said: al-ghurfah is Paradise. "For what they endured" means: for their patience in obeying their Lord and obeying their Prophet, upon him be the best of prayers and peace. Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn said: "for what they endured" refers to patience in poverty and destitution in this world. Al-Dahhak said: "for what they endured" refers to restraint from desires.

(And they will be met therein with greeting and peace.) The rest read "wa-yulaqqawna" and this was preferred by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, because of His words: "And He gave them radiance and joy." (Abiding therein.) Accusative as a circumstantial state. (Excellent is it as a dwelling place and a station.)

His words, may He be exalted: (Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication.) This is a difficult verse which the heretics have seized upon. "As if upon his breast and on his two sides was musk, which a bride's perfume-applier arranges, layer upon layer."

This is supported by the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr and others. It was said: "ma ya'ba'u bikum" means: with the forgiveness of your sins, and it is not great in His sight, "were it not for your supplication" with Him of the gods and partners. Its evidence: "What would Allah do with your punishment if you are thankful and believe," said al-Dahhak. Ibn Munabbih related that it was in the Torah: "O son of Adam, by My might, I did not create you to profit from you; I created you so that you might profit from Me. So take Me in place of everything, for I am better for you than everything." The original is: "were it not for your calling upon other than Him as gods," and the response of "law la" is omitted, its estimate in this view being: He would not have punished you. Its parallel is His words: "Indeed, those you call upon besides Allah are servants like you."

(Then you have denied.) That is, you denied what you were called to; this is according to the first view, and you denied the oneness of Allah according to the second.

(Then it will be inevitable.) That is, your denial will be binding upon you. The meaning: the reward of denial will be, as He said: "And they will find what they did present," meaning the reward of what they did; and His words: "So taste the punishment because you disbelieved," meaning the reward of what you disbelieved. The omission of "denial" is good because its verb has been mentioned, for when you mention the verb it indicates its verbal noun by its form, as He said: "Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them," meaning, belief would have been better.
