Al-Tabari said: "lizaman" means a lasting, binding punishment and a destroying ruin that joins some of you to others, like the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb: "So a sudden attack struck him..." [[al-'adiyah: people who run on foot; that is, their assault clung to him as those who cling to what they are in and do not part from it. He likened their assault to the collapse of a pool when it collapses. Another reading has:]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verses 74–77 (part 2 of 2):

فلم ير غير عادية لزاما]] [Then he did not see other than ʿādiyah (?) lizāman]]

﴿Lizāman, as the deep pit that collapses ...﴾ *kamā yatafajjaru al-ḥawḍ al-laqīf* ("as the pool that has been breached bursts"). He means by *al-lizām* that which follows one another, and by *al-laqīf* the one whose stones have fallen and collapsed.

Al-Nahhas: Abu Hatim related from Abu Zayd, who said: "I heard Qu'nub Abu al-Sammal reading *lazāman* with a fatḥah on the lām." Abu Ja'far said: It would be the verbal noun of *lazima* (to be bound to), but the kasrah is preferable, being like *qitāl* and *muqātalah* (both verbal nouns of fighting). The community agreed on the kasrah in the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Had it not been for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord, it would have been inevitable (*lizām*), and a specified term.﴾

Others said: *al-lizām* with a kasrah is the verbal noun of *lāzama* (to constantly attend to), like *khāṣama* with *khiṣām*; and *al-lizām* with a fatḥah is the verbal noun of *lazima*, like *salima* with *salāman*, meaning *salāmah* (soundness). So *al-lizām* with a fatḥah is *al-luzūm* (the state of being bound), and *al-lizām* with a kasrah is *al-mulāzamah* (constant adherence). In both readings the verbal noun has taken the place of the active participle: *lizām* stands in place of *mulāzim* (constantly adhering), and *lizām* stands in place of *lāzim* (necessary). As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should sink away (*ghawran*)?﴾, meaning *ghā'iran* (sunken).

Al-Nahhas said: Al-Farra' has a view concerning the subject (*ism*) of *yakūn*. He said: it is *majhūl* (unidentified). This is an error, because the predicate of an unidentified subject can only be a clause, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears [Allah] and is patient...﴾, and as the grammarians have related: *kāna Zaydun munṭaliqun*, where the subject is *Zaydun* and its predicate is *munṭaliqun*. The grammarians also say that the subject of *kāna* is an implied pronoun, and the estimate is *kāna al-ḥadīth* (the matter was). As for saying *kāna munṭaliqan* with an unidentified subject in *kāna*, this is not permitted according to anyone we know of.

And success is from Allah, He is the One sought for help, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

This is like his words, upon him be prayers and peace, to Anas: "O Allah, increase his wealth and his offspring, and bless him in them," whose explanation has been given previously in Al 'Imran and Maryam. That is because when a person is blessed in his wealth and offspring, his eyes are comforted by his family and dependents. "How many a comforted eye was heated yesterday, and eyes were made cool whose tears now flow."

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And make us leaders for the righteous﴾, meaning, exemplars who are followed in good. Some said: he meant a'immah, just as the speaker says "these are our commander" meaning "our commanders." The poet said:
"O my blamers, do not increase my reproach; the blamers are not commanders over me,"
meaning, not commanders (umara'). Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: they did not seek leadership, but to be exemplars in religion. Ibn 'Abbas said: make us leaders of guidance, as He said: "And We made among them leaders guiding by Our command." Makhul said: make us leaders in piety whom the righteous follow. It was said: this is of the inverted construction, its meaning being: "and make the righteous a leader for us," this was said by Mujahid. (Abiding therein.) Accusative as a circumstantial state. (Excellent is it as a dwelling place and a station.)

His words, may He be exalted: (Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication.) This is a difficult verse which the heretics have seized upon. It is said: "ma 'abi'tu bi-fulan," meaning I did not care for so-and-so, that is, he had no weight or value with me. The root of ya'ba' is from al-'ibe', which is burden. The poet said:

Its evidence: "So when they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion," and the like. Its evidence: "What would Allah do with your punishment if you are thankful and believe," said al-Dahhak. Ibn Munabbih related that it was in the Torah: "O son of Adam, by My might, I did not create you to profit from you; I created you so that you might profit from Me. So take Me in place of everything, for I am better for you than everything." Ibn Jinni said: Ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn 'Abbas read "fa-qad kadhdhaba al-kafirun." al-Zahrawi and al-Nahhas said: it is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and it is explanatory, the ta' and mim in "kadhdhabtum" being explanatory. Al-Qutaybi and al-Farisi held that the supplication is attributed to its subject, and the object is omitted. The original is: "were it not for your calling upon other than Him as gods," and the response of "law la" is omitted, its estimate in this view being: He would not have punished you. Its parallel is His words: "Indeed, those you call upon besides Allah are servants like you."

(Then you have denied.) That is, you denied what you were called to; this is according to the first view, and you denied the oneness of Allah according to the second.

(Then it will be inevitable.) That is, your denial will be binding upon you. The meaning: the reward of denial will be, as He said: "And they will find what they did present," meaning the reward of what they did; and His words: "So taste the punishment because you disbelieved," meaning the reward of what you disbelieved. The omission of "denial" is good because its verb has been mentioned, for when you mention the verb it indicates its verbal noun by its form, as He said: "Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them," meaning, belief would have been better. It will come explained in Surah al-Dukhan, Allah willing. Another group said: it is a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter. Also from Ibn Mas'ud: lizam is the denial itself, meaning they will not be given repentance from it, as related by al-Zahrawi. Thus the Day of Badr and other punishments that they are bound to are included in this. Abu 'Ubaydah said: lizaman means decisive, meaning: it will be a decisive matter between you and the believers. This is supported by the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr and others. "Then you have denied" — the address with "ya'ba'" is to all people, then He says to Quraysh: you have denied and not worshipped Him, so denial will surely be the cause of the punishment that clings to you. Al-Naqqash and others said: the meaning is, were it not for your calling upon Him in distresses and the like. Its evidence: "So when they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion," and the like. It was said: "ma ya'ba'u bikum" means: with the forgiveness of your sins, and it is not great in His sight, "were it not for your supplication" with Him of the gods and partners. Its evidence: "What would Allah do with your punishment if you are thankful and believe," said al-Dahhak. Al-Walid ibn Abi al-Walid said: it reached me that in it [the meaning is]: I did not create you while I had need of you, except that you ask Me and I forgive you and give you. Ibn Munabbih related that it was in the Torah: "O son of Adam, by My might, I did not create you to profit from you; I created you so that you might profit from Me. So take Me in place of everything, for I am better for you than everything." Ibn Jinni said: Ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn 'Abbas read "fa-qad kadhdhaba al-kafirun." al-Zahrawi and al-Nahhas said: it is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and it is explanatory, the ta' and mim in "kadhdhabtum" being explanatory. Al-Qutaybi and al-Farisi held that the supplication is attributed to its subject, and the object is omitted. The original is: "were it not for your calling upon other than Him as gods," and the response of "law la" is omitted, its estimate in this view being: He would not have punished you. Its parallel is His words: "Indeed, those you call upon besides Allah are servants like you."

(Then you have denied.) That is, you denied what you were called to; this is according to the first view, and you denied the oneness of Allah according to the second.

(Then it will be inevitable.) That is, your denial will be binding upon you. The meaning: the reward of denial will be, as He said: "And they will find what they did present," meaning the reward of what they did; and His words: "So taste the punishment because you disbelieved," meaning the reward of what you disbelieved. The omission of "denial" is good because its verb has been mentioned, for when you mention the verb it indicates its verbal noun by its form, as He said: "Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them," meaning, belief would have been better. And His words: "If you are grateful, He is pleased with it for you," meaning He is pleased with gratitude. Similar examples are many. The majority of exegetes hold that what is meant by "lizam" (inevitability) here is what befell them on the day of Badr. This is the view of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Malik, Mujahid, Muqatil and others. In Sahih Muslim, from 'Abd Allah: "The seizing, the smoke and the lizam have passed." It will come explained in Surah al-Dukhan, Allah willing. Another group said: it is a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter. Also from Ibn Mas'ud: lizam is the denial itself, meaning they will not be given repentance from it, as related by al-Zahrawi. Thus the Day of Badr and other punishments that they are bound to are included in this. Abu 'Ubaydah said: lizaman means decisive, meaning: it will be a decisive matter between you and the believers. Most readers recite with a kasrah on the lam, and Abu 'Ubaydah recited for Sakhr: "If they escape the collapse of the earth, they have met their deaths inevitably." "Lizaman" and "mulazamah" are one. Al-Tabari said: "lizaman" means a lasting, binding punishment and a destroying ruin that joins some of you to others, like the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb: "So a sudden attack struck him..." [[al-'adiyah: people who run on foot; that is, their assault clung to him as those who cling to what they are in and do not part from it. He likened their assault to the collapse of a pool when it collapses. Another reading has:]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 25, verses 74–77 (part 2 of 2):

فلم ير غير عادية لزاما]] [Then he did not see other than ʿādiyah (?) lizāman]]

﴿Lizāman, as the deep pit that collapses ...﴾ *kamā yatafajjaru al-ḥawḍ al-laqīf* ("as the pool that has been breached bursts"). He means by *al-lizām* that which follows one another, and by *al-laqīf* the one whose stones have fallen and collapsed.

Al-Nahhas: Abu Hatim related from Abu Zayd, who said: "I heard Qu'nub Abu al-Sammal reading *lazāman* with a fatḥah on the lām." Abu Ja'far said: It would be the verbal noun of *lazima* (to be bound to), but the kasrah is preferable, being like *qitāl* and *muqātalah* (both verbal nouns of fighting). The community agreed on the kasrah in the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Had it not been for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord, it would have been inevitable (*lizām*), and a specified term.﴾

Others said: *al-lizām* with a kasrah is the verbal noun of *lāzama* (to constantly attend to), like *khāṣama* with *khiṣām*; and *al-lizām* with a fatḥah is the verbal noun of *lazima*, like *salima* with *salāman*, meaning *salāmah* (soundness). So *al-lizām* with a fatḥah is *al-luzūm* (the state of being bound), and *al-lizām* with a kasrah is *al-mulāzamah* (constant adherence). In both readings the verbal noun has taken the place of the active participle: *lizām* stands in place of *mulāzim* (constantly adhering), and *lizām* stands in place of *lāzim* (necessary). As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should sink away (*ghawran*)?﴾, meaning *ghā'iran* (sunken).

Al-Nahhas said: Al-Farra' has a view concerning the subject (*ism*) of *yakūn*. He said: it is *majhūl* (unidentified). This is an error, because the predicate of an unidentified subject can only be a clause, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears [Allah] and is patient...﴾, and as the grammarians have related: *kāna Zaydun munṭaliqun*, where the subject is *Zaydun* and its predicate is *munṭaliqun*. The grammarians also say that the subject of *kāna* is an implied pronoun, and the estimate is *kāna al-ḥadīth* (the matter was). As for saying *kāna munṭaliqan* with an unidentified subject in *kāna*, this is not permitted according to anyone we know of.

And success is from Allah, He is the One sought for help, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
